data.title: The 4 Stages Of DJIA And What's Next
data.description:
The four stages: what they are and where they come from

Every traded asset moves through four phases, and knowing which one it is in tells you a lot about what to do. That is the idea behind Stan Weinstein's stage analysis, laid out in his 1988 book Secrets for Profiting in Bull and Bear Markets. Weinstein watched a stock's price against its 30-week moving average and named four stages:

  • Stage 1, basing: after a decline, the price goes sideways around a flattening average while sellers run out.

  • Stage 2, advancing: the price breaks out above a rising average and keeps making higher highs. This is the stage he wanted to own.

  • Stage 3, topping: the advance stalls, the price churns around the average, and the average rolls over.

  • Stage 4, declining: the price falls below a falling average. This is the stage he wanted to avoid or sell short.

His rule of thumb was simple: buy when a stock moves from Stage 1 into Stage 2, hold while it stays there, and get out before Stage 4 does the damage.

How I use them here

Weinstein read his stages by eye, judging the shape of the base or the top. To back-test them I need a definition a computer can apply the same way every day, so I use two tests: is the close above or below the 200-day moving average (about 40 weeks, a little slower than his 30), and the slope of that average.

In this version, Stage 1 is a close below a rising average, Stage 2 a close above a rising average, Stage 3 a close above a falling average, and Stage 4 a close below a falling average.

One difference matters for this article. In Weinstein's version, Stage 1 comes after a decline. In this mechanical version, any close below a still-rising average counts as Stage 1, so it also catches the first days of a pullback inside an uptrend, before anyone knows whether it is a dip or the start of a top. Since 1928 the Dow has spent about 60% of its trading days in Stage 2, 24% in Stage 4, and about 8% each in Stages 1 and 3. Stage 1 is the rarest and the most ambiguous: a pullback in an uptrend and the start of a bear market look exactly alike there.

The stages are not a trading signal on their own. Here they work as a filter for one: my dip buys, the CIT Oscillator crossing back up from oversold, are taken only when the asset is in Stage 2.

Why it matters this month

This month the Dow, the S&P 500, the Nasdaq 100 and the Russell 2000 all slipped out of Stage 2 and into Stage 1. The Dow closed Friday at 48,147, 5.2% below its 200-day average of 50,776, but that average is still rising. So the practical question is whether this is a dip to buy or a time to wait.

My rules wait. The rest of this article lays out why, in five steps: what each stage has done for the Dow since 1928, how oversold buys fared in each stage across 36 assets since 2001, how long the Dow has stayed below its 200-day average once it breaks, whether heavy NYSE selling changes the picture, and how to hold on to more of a Stage 2 advance than a short dip trade captures.

What each stage has done on its own

Start with the plain record: the Dow's average return over the next 20, 60 and 250 trading days from every day in each stage. The figure in brackets is the share of times the Dow was higher.

Stage 4 has been the weakest over the following one to three months, as you'd expect. Stage 1 is the interesting one, because it has changed character. Since 1976, a Dow in Stage 1 rose an average of 3.62% over the next 60 days and was higher 76% of the time, the best of any stage. From 1928 to 1975 the same setup averaged +0.07% and was higher only 46% of the time, the worst. A dip below a still-rising average has been a gift in the modern era and a trap in the 1930s and early 1970s.

Dip buys by stage

A trader's question is narrower: when an oversold signal fires, does the stage matter? I ran every CIT Oscillator buy (a cross back up through 25) on the 30 Dow stocks plus SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA, GLD and TLT from 2001 to November 2026, with no filter except the stage on the signal day. Each trade was entered at the next open and closed when the oscillator dropped back below 75. Prices are adjusted for dividends and splits.

Splitting the record into two eras, as in the lower half of the chart, tells more than the totals:

  • Stage 2 was solid in both: a profit factor of 1.38 in 2001-2012 and 1.75 in 2013-2026, with the fewest large losses.

  • Stage 4 flipped: it lost money in 2001-2012 (profit factor 0.97, with 14% of trades losing 10% or more), then did well in the V-shaped markets since 2013 (2.02). A filter can't count on the next bear market being V-shaped.

  • Stage 1 worked, but less well than Stage 2 in both eras: 1.23 and 1.58, with more large losses.

·       Stage 3 looks best but is thin: 153 trades across 36 assets in 25 years, most of the result from 2013-2026. That is too few to build a rule on.

Why the rules buy only in Stage 2

Stage 2 isn't chosen for having the single best number in a table. It's chosen because it is where most dip buys happen, it held up in every period I tested, and it keeps you out of the stretches that do real damage.

The long Dow test shows how. Running the full rules on the Dow from 1928 to 2026, requiring Stage 2 raised the profit factor from 1.46 to 1.76, and nearly all of that difference came from 1929-1945. Buying oversold dips during the 1929-1932 collapse lost money without the filter (profit factor 0.72) and made money with it (2.34). In most other eras the results with and without the filter were close. On the ETFs since 2005, dropping the filter added about 15% more trades with similar results.

So the filter works like insurance: it costs a few trades in normal markets and pays off in the rare long bear market. Stage 1 is where that trade-off is decided, because every Stage 4 decline from an uptrend starts as a Stage 1 dip. That makes the next question the important one: once the Dow breaks below its 200-day average, how long does it usually stay there?

Days below the 200-day average: most breaks are brief, but some aren't

Next, I looked at how long a break below the 200 dma lasted. And the answer is that most breaks don’t last. The median break lasted three trading days, and four out of five were over within a month. On its own, a close below the 200-day average has said very little, which is why Stage 1 dips have usually been good buys since 1976.

Back above the line is not the same as recovered

A tougher test is how long the Dow took to close back at its high of the 12 months before the break. Across all 250 breaks the median was about 166 trading days, roughly eight months.

The picture changes once a break lasts. Twenty-six breaks kept the Dow below its 200-day average for 60 trading days or more, and for those the median wait to regain the prior high was about 420 trading days, or 1.7 years.

What stands out

  • Fast recoveries are common even among the long breaks. Seven of the 21 episodes regained the prior high within about a year: 1968, 1982, 1984, 1990, 2011, 2015 and 2020.

  • The depth of the drop doesn't decide the wait. The 2020 crash fell 37% and was back in eight months; the 1977 break fell 27% and took 4.2 years.

  • The long waits cluster in two eras. The 1966-1982 stretch of inflation and high rates and the 2000-2013 stretch of the dot-com bust and the financial crisis account for every recovery longer than 3.5 years. Outside those eras, no break took more than two years.

On the first day of a break there is no way to tell which kind it will be. Stage 2 rules don't try to guess. They wait for a close back above a rising average, which means missing the early part of some quick recoveries in exchange for never averaging down into the 1929, 1973 or 2008 kind of break.

Does heavy selling change the picture?

There may be one exception worth knowing. Does a burst of heavy NYSE selling make a dip buy worth taking outside Stage 2? The evidence shows that a single heavy-selling day says little outside Stage 2. In Stage 2 it was followed by gains 73% of the time; in Stages 1 and 4 it was a coin flip.

  • A cluster of heavy-selling days is different. It was followed by above-average gains in every stage, which looks more like capitulation than trend. In Stage 1, SPY was higher five days later in 16 of 17 cases. In Stage 4 the bounce came only after the deepest dips (an average worst low of -7.1% within 20 days).

  • A cluster turned Stage 4 dip buys from losers into winners. Oscillator buys in Stage 4 averaged -0.50% over 20 days. The 21 that came within 10 days of a selling cluster averaged +2.12%, and +6.23% over 60 days. The improvement held in both 2001-2013 and 2014-2026.

The samples are small, so I treat this as a possible exception, not a new rule: heavy, repeated selling is the one condition where buying below the 200-day average has held up. Without it, Stage 2 remains the place to buy dips.

Beyond the short trade: riding the whole Stage 2

The dip buys above are short trades, about two to three weeks from the oversold signal back to the top of the range. A Stage 2 advance often lasts a year or more, so the natural follow-up is how to stay in for more of it. I tested several entries and exits on the same 36 assets from 2001 to 2026.

Together the tests suggest a two-part plan for Stage 2. The core position goes on early in a new Stage 2, on the fifth straight Stage 2 day or the first oscillator buy, and is held until Stage 4. Every later oscillator buy is a separate short-term trade, closed when the oscillator falls back below 75, rather than an addition to the core.

Where the market stands now

All four moved straight from Stage 2 into Stage 1 this month: QQQ and IWM on November 13, the Dow on November 17 and SPY on November 19. The Dow's break is four trading days old, in the range where 56% of breaks since 1956 have ended. Duration is the thing to watch, more than depth: if the Dow is still below its average by mid-February 2027, about 60 trading days in, it would join the group where recoveries took years rather than months. Before that, two levels decide what comes next:

  • Back to Stage 2: a close back above the 200-day average, now about 50,776. Dip-buy signals would count again from there.

  • On to Stage 4: the average itself turning down. The closes now dropping out of the 200-day window, from February and early March, were mostly between 47,500 and 50,200. If the Dow simply stayed near 48,150, the average would fall below its level of 20 days earlier in about 11 trading days, in early December. That would make it Stage 4, the stage where dip buys lost money in 2001-2012 and where the Dow's next three months have been weakest.

The selling side is already notable. NYSE down volume was 80% on November 12, 78% on November 16 and 79% on November 17, which completed a selling cluster while SPY was still in Stage 2. On November 19, the day SPY slipped into Stage 1, 86% of NYSE volume was in declining stocks. Clusters in Stage 1 have had some of the better follow-throughs in the record, but with 17 cases since 2001 that is a tendency, not a forecast.

Until the Dow closes back above a rising 200-day average, it is in Stage 1. Oversold signals are worth watching there but, under strict rules, not buying.

data.title: Rising Memory Costs Could Give China's Used-Phone Market A New Tailwind
data.description:
I’ve followed ATRenew (NYSE: RERE) for a few years. While it has always had a great growth story, I am more confident in the company now than ever. Beyond its strong financial performance, the rise of AI is now a major tailwind for the pre-owned electronics market. As ATRenew’s CEO noted on the recent earnings call, the growing cost of chips and memory is driving new smartphone prices, particularly new iPhones and computers, to climb. Because pre-owned electronics sales are ATRenew’s largest revenue stream, rising retail prices create a substantial opportunity for the company.

Its Q3’2026 results, released yesterday, were better than I expected. Revenue continued to grow at a healthy pace, profitability improved considerably faster than sales, and the company is returning a meaningful amount of capital to shareholders through buybacks. More importantly, several developments in the consumer electronics market could work in its favor over the coming quarters.

I think investors may be overlooking an interesting combination here: a growing secondhand electronics market, improving operating efficiency, and a management team that is increasingly focused on shareholder returns.

Now let’s dive deeper into its Q3 results. ATRenew reported third-quarter revenue of RMB 6.45 billion, up 25.3% YoY. That was slightly above the upper end of management's previous guidance of RMB 6.3 to 6.4 billion. Product revenue, which accounts for the bulk of the business, increased 27% to RMB 6 billion. Service revenue grew at a slower 6.1% to RMB 448.7 million, supported by the PJT Marketplace and multi-category recycling business.

What I find more encouraging is that profit growth outpaced revenue growth. GAAP operating income increased 58% to RMB 190.7 million, while adjusted operating income rose 50.7% to RMB 211.5 million. The adjusted operating margin reached 3.3%, compared with 2.7% a year earlier. GAAP net income increased 53.6% to RMB 139.5 million. These are meaningful improvements for a business that historically operated on relatively thin margins. Management attributed the progress partly to better fulfillment and marketing efficiency as the company benefits from greater operating scale.

The Q4 outlook is also encouraging. ATRenew expects revenue of RMB7.8 to 7.9 billion, representing growth of approximately 24% to 26%. Based on the nine-month revenue already reported, this would put full-year 2026 revenue at around RMB 27.0 to 27.1 billion. The important point is that growth is not coming at the expense of profitability. That is something I want to see continue.

As I mentioned at the beginning of the article, one development worth watching is the sharp increase in memory prices. AI infrastructure spending has increased demand for high-bandwidth memory and conventional DRAM, while supply allocation and production capacity have become more complicated. Gartner has also forecast significant increases in smartphone and PC prices during 2026 as memory and storage costs feed into hardware pricing. This matters to ATRenew because the economics of buying and selling used electronics are closely linked to the price of new products. When a new smartphone becomes more expensive, consumers have another reason to consider pre-owned ones. I would not assume that every increase in new-phone prices translates directly into a company's profit as consumers trading in their devices will likely demand higher payout values as well. Demand, inventory turnover, competitive landscape and customer experience still matter a lot. But the pricing environment could be favorable for a company with ATRenew's sourcing network and distribution capabilities.

The company transacted 12 million consumer products in Q3, compared with 10.9 million a year earlier. This is a useful indicator of platform activity, although it measures transactions across distribution channels rather than unique devices collected. For ATRenew, the opportunity is not simply to sell more used phones. It is to improve the economics of each transaction while making secondhand products more attractive to consumers.

Another part of the business I find encouraging is the expansion of its direct-to-consumer operations. ATRenew's 1P2C business grew 44.3% during the quarter, increasing its contribution to product revenue from 36.4% to 41.4%. This matters because selling directly to consumers gives the company more control over the retail experience and potentially allows it to capture more of the value generated along the distribution chain. 

The improvement in gross margin supports the argument. First-party gross margin increased to 14.4% from 13.4% a year earlier.Another growth driver is international expansion. ATRenew's overseas business is still relatively small, but growth has been impressive. International product revenue reached approximately RMB240 million in Q3, representing growth of around 150% YoY. Management is targeting RMB 1 billion in overseas revenue for the full year. The company has also expanded its international trading infrastructure, including a Dubai hub that began trial operations in October.

This opportunity is fairly straightforward. China has a large and increasingly sophisticated supply chain for pre-owned electronics. ATRenew can leverage that infrastructure to source, assess and distribute devices into overseas markets where affordable smartphones and consumer electronics remain in demand. 

Of course, the overseas business is still small, accounting for only around 4% of first-party product revenue. It also declined sequentially in Q3 due to seasonal supply conditions and softer B2B trading activity. I would not build an aggressive valuation around international expansion just yet. But if ATRenew can replicate its sourcing, quality-control and distribution capabilities outside China, this could become one of the strongest growth drivers over time.

The last piece I want to discuss is liquidity. Growth stocks are often valued primarily on revenue expansion, but ultimately shareholders want to see profits translate into cash and returns on capital. ATRenew had RMB 1.94 billion in cash and cash equivalents, restricted cash, short-term investments and funds receivable from third party payment service providers as of September 30, 2026. This provides meaningful financial flexibility, and more importantly, management is putting capital returns into practice.

During Q3, the company repurchased approximately 1.6 million ADSs for US 6.6 million. Since the current repurchase program began, cumulative buybacks have reached US 21.4 million, with another US 28.6 million available.

There is also a broader commitment that investors should not overlook. ATRenew has reaffirmed its shareholder return plan for fiscal years 2025 to 2027. Under this plan, the company intends to return at least 60% of annual adjusted net income to shareholders through share repurchases, cash dividends or a combination of the two. If earnings continue to expand, the potential for buybacks and dividends becomes increasingly interesting. I particularly like the fact that management is not treating shareholder returns as an afterthought. It is becoming part of the company's capital allocation strategy.

Overall, I think ATRenew is becoming a more interesting business than its current valuation suggests. The Q3 results show that revenue growth is translating into stronger operating profitability. Its direct retail business is gaining share, international operations are expanding, and management is making a tangible effort to return capital to shareholders. The memory-price environment provides an additional potential tailwind. Of course, there are risks that should not be ignored.  International expansion will take time, and competition in China's pre-owned electronics market remains significant. The company also needs to demonstrate that earnings growth is consistently translating into free cash flow. However, at current valuations, I think the stock is worth a closer look.

data.title: Target Shines, Walmart Merely Fine: Two Retail Giants Split On Q3 Results
data.description:
Walmart (WMT - Free Report) shares were down after Thursday's Q3 results, but they were among the few to be in the green on Friday in a broadly down day for the market. Unlike Target (TGT - Free Report), which had come out with truly impressive results Wednesday morning, Walmart’s results were ok; not great, but not bad either.

As we noted about Walmart shares recently, their defensive attributes position them to stand their ground during periods of market turmoil. Market participants are clearly grappling with some weighty questions about the broader AI space, with even the long-awaited Anthropic (ANT - Free Report) stock losing ground the day after its successful debut. 

Walmart shares’ recent struggles notwithstanding, they have outperformed peers like Target (TGT - Free Report) and even Amazon (AMZN - Free Report) over the last five years, up more than +184.2% vs. +38.5% for Amazon and -19.4% for Target. Walmart’s +184.2% gain over the last five years compares to a +69.2% gain for the S&P 500 index.

Unlike this standout performance over the last five years, Walmart shares seem to have lost their mojo this year, even though they appear to be rebounding lately, as the year-to-date performance chart below for Walmart, Target, Amazon, and the S&P 500 index shows.

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

Walmart shares fell sharply after the last quarterly release on August 20th, reflecting a combination of factors, including a seemingly lower-quality earnings beat (benefiting from tariff refunds), decelerating comp growth, and underwhelming Q3 guidance.

Walmart and other big-box retailers are undoubtedly facing a difficult operating environment, with elevated fuel costs not only adding to consumers’ financial burdens but also increasing retailers’ expenses. Walmart noted on the Q3 earnings call that elevated diesel and transportation costs have added $2 billion to their cost base this year.

A big worry among Walmart investors is decelerating same-store sales or comp growth, which came in at +2.9% for Q3 vs. +2.6% in Q2 and +4.1% in Q1. Comps were north of +4% in each of the preceding year’s quarters.

Target appears to have firmly put its struggles of the last couple of years behind it, with Q3 comps coming in at +5.6% (vs. estimates of +3.07%). This was the third quarter in a row that Target posted better-than-expected comps.

It is important to keep in mind that Walmart shares command a premium valuation, trading at 40X forward 12-month EPS estimates, only modestly below the 10-year high of 45.4X in February 2026. This represents a significant expansion in the valuation premium relative to Target, as the chart below of the two stocks’ 10-year valuation history shows

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

Market participants expect stocks with premium valuation multiples to beat and raise when they report results, which is not what we have been seeing from Walmart lately.

Despite the negative effects of elevated fuel costs on consumer spending and the company’s freight costs, Walmart remains better positioned than many others in the space given its value orientation, greater indexing to groceries, and robust digital capabilities. Walmart has consistently gained market share among higher-income households in recent years, which has more than offset affordability-driven softness among lower-income consumers.

With respect to the Retail sector 2026 Q3 earnings season scorecard, we now have results from 24 of the 30 retailers in the S&P 500 index. Regular readers know that Zacks has a dedicated stand-alone economic sector for retail, unlike its placement in the Consumer Staples and Consumer Discretionary sectors in the Standard & Poor’s standard industry classification. The Zacks Retail sector includes not only Walmart, Target, and other traditional retailers, but also online vendors like Amazon and restaurant players.

Total Q3 earnings for these 24 retailers that have reported are up +3.5% from the same period last year on +8.4% higher revenues, with 75% beating EPS estimates and 66.7% beating revenue estimates.

Please note that the Zacks Retail sector’s Q3 EPS and revenue beats percentages at 75% and 66.7% are meaningfully below the corresponding Q3 EPS and revenue beats percentages for the S&P 500 index as a whole at 82.3% and 75.9%, respectively.

The comparison charts below put the Q3 beats percentages for these retailers in a historical context.

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

As you can see above, the Retail sector’s Q3 revenue beats percentages are tracking below the historical averages for this group of companies, while the sector’s Q3 EPS beats are in line with the 20-quarter average.

With respect to earnings and revenue growth rates at this stage, we like to show the group’s performance with and without Amazon, whose results are among the 24 companies that have already reported. As we know, Amazon’s Q3 earnings were down -2.4% on +12.1% higher revenues, as it missed both EPS and top- line expectations. 

The two comparison charts below show the Q3 earnings and revenue growth relative to other recent periods, both with Amazon’s results (left side chart) and without Amazon’s numbers (right side chart)

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

As you can see above, earnings for the group outside of Amazon are up +8.2% on a +6.9% top-line gain.

Looking at Q3 for the Zacks Retail sector as a whole, combining the actual results that have come out with estimates for the still-to-come retailers, total earnings for the sector are expected to increase by +3.3% from the same period last year on +8% higher revenues.

For 2026, Zacks Retail sector earnings are expected to increase by +7.6%, with 2027 earnings expected to increase by +21.6%. Excluding Amazon’s contribution, earnings growth for the Zacks Retail sector is expected to be +6.9% this year ( vs. +7.6% with Amazon) and +9.7% next year (vs. +21.6% otherwise).

Q3 Earnings Season Scorecard

Through Friday, November 20th, we have seen Q3 results from 468 S&P 500 members, or 93.6% of the index’s total membership. Total earnings for these companies are up +28.9% from the same period last year on +14.3% higher revenues, with 82.3% beating EPS estimates and 75.9% beating revenue estimates.

The comparison charts below show the earnings and revenue growth rates for these companies compared to other recent periods.

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

Excluding the Nvidia (NVDA - Free Report), Micron (MU - Free Report), and Alphabet (GOOGL - Free Report) contributions, Q3 earnings for the remaining index members that have reported would be up +21.5%.

The comparison charts below show Q3 earnings and revenue growth for this group of companies, excluding Nvidia, Micron, and Alphabet, across all periods.

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

The comparison charts below show the Q3 EPS and revenue beat percentages for these companies compared to other recent periods.

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

The Earnings Big Picture

Looking at Q3 as a whole, combining the actual results from the 468 S&P 500 members with estimates for the still-to-come companies, total earnings are on track to increase by +29.8% from the same period last year on +14.9% higher revenues, as the chart below shows.

As you can see above, the expectation is that index earnings will increase by +28.3% from the same period last year on +13.6% higher revenues in the current period (2026 Q4).

The revisions trend has been positive, as we have repeatedly noted in this note in recent weeks and as the chart below shows.

We should note that the magnitude of positive revisions we are seeing for Q4 is weaker than what we saw in the comparable period for Q3.

The chart below shows the aggregate growth picture for the S&P 500 index on a calendar year basis.

Nvidia, Micron, and Alphabet have substantial weight in the index's annual earnings growth pace as a whole. The chart below shows the substantial contribution of these three Tech players to the index’s earnings growth pace.

data.title: Bitcoin Below $58K As Stablecoin Supply Shrinks $14-17B In A Month
data.description:
Bitcoin (BTC.X) fell below $58,000 on 20 November 2026 after sweeping through the $59,000 to $62,000 liquidation cluster that had sat on the market since August, and the squeeze came as the industry’s own liquidity was draining: stablecoin supply contracted by $14 billion to $17 billion in the 30 days before the break, per Glassnode’s data.

Both liquidity rails dried up at once

The stablecoin contraction matters because stablecoins are the funding side of the futures market. While their supply shrank through November, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded combined net outflows of more than $1.1 billion over the Tuesday-to-Thursday sessions, by Farside Investors data. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) alone lost $541.1 million on Thursday, 19 November, its largest single-day outflow since launch, inside a $582.3 million day for the ETF complex as a whole, even as Q3 13F filings showed endowments holding their IBIT stakes. The 19 November record topped the previous daily outflow high, which Farside data dates to January. Price and flows moved together. CoinGecko data put the low at $57,700 on 20 November, the first break below $60,000 since June, with other tracking showing the session closing near $58,300 to $59,500. Bitcoin had traded above $86,000 in September before a three-month pattern of lower highs and lower lows. Banks had been adding to ETF positions through the third quarter, so the November withdrawal wave marked a sharp turn in institutional behaviour.

What the desks are watching

Glassnode’s 17 November weekly report, ‘Capitulation Meets Support’, flagged the $59,000 to $62,000 zone as the largest liquidation cluster on its six-month futures heatmap, tracing it mostly to leveraged longs opened in August 2026. On 21 November, the firm confirmed the cluster had been fully cleared the day before. It also identified the largest bids since August at $60,000 and below, and warned that a daily close beneath a $62,000 to $66,000 band of recently acquired coins could open a decline toward $53,700. QCP Capital framed the wider conditions: “A meaningful recovery likely needs tech equities to stabilise, rates volatility to fall and institutional flows to return.” A U.S. tech stock index fell to its lowest level since April amid the broader selloff, the backdrop QCP pointed to for why short-covering rallies may struggle until those conditions change. Sentiment echoed the flush. Santiment measured Bitcoin’s bullish-to-bearish social media comment ratio at 0.59 on 20 November, an ‘Extreme Fear’ reading continuing a collapse in crowd confidence that began around mid-September. For traders sizing risk into the next session, the levels in play are $60,000 and below, where Glassnode sees the heaviest bids, and the $53,700 downside trigger.

data.title: AI Is The First Bubble Of Bubbles
data.description:
Below are some of the most interesting things I came across this week.

CHART

It’s popular to say that financial bubbles can only be identified well after the fact. But FT Alphaville highlights a study that shows the media, in aggregate, is actually pretty good at spotting bubbles in real time. “Almost every time these lines have ticked above 50 per cent, it has coincided with a historically recognised bubble, which has, before too long, popped.”

CHART

As Paul Kedrosky notes, ‘The current moment is unusual in that is at the intersection of all four bubbleish forces, having credit, government, real estate, and technology drivers. But this feedback loop also makes the current moment uniquely fragile.’

STAT

What changed recently is that the AI Bubble lost its circular financing engine. Pitchbook reports, “For years, the AI world has benefited from a cash machine like no other. Nvidia (NVDA), whose chips power much of the more than $1 trillion expected to flow into AI this year, has used its windfalls to rain down capital on every conceivable piece of the AI value chain.”

LINK

Wall Street analysts remain resolutely bullish. But, as Joachim Klement points out, “Wall Street analysts were overwhelmingly bullish at the peak of the 1990s tech bubble and on the eve of the 2008 global financial crisis.”

LINK

Ratings agencies, too, remain sanguine about the creditworthiness of the major AI players in spite of credit markets signaling otherwise. But they were just as sanguine about the major banks in the lead up to the Great Financial Crisis. To paraphrase Groundbreaker, ‘Every major AI lessee and guarantor’s market-implied credit rating sits four to seven notches below its agency rating, 5.3 on average. Wall Street’s broker-dealers showed the same gap in 2007.’

Going by the CME FedWatch gauge, futures traders are pricing in a 25-basis-point increase next month, followed by one more of similar increment by next March.

Two others – Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack – dissented in favor of a 25-basis-point increase in a 10-2 vote. In a rather interesting twist, Governor Christopher Waller of late has been stating that the FOMC, the rate-setting body, should consider 50 basis points next month.

The hawks are clearly worried about how inflation is progressing. Consumer inflation has remained above the Federal Reserve’s stated goal of two percent for over five years now. Both headline and core CPI (consumer price index) in October rose 0.4 percent month over month, and the readings were 0.1 percentage point higher than the consensus.

Next month’s meeting, slated for 8-9, hence can be market moving. A 25-basis-point increase is just about guaranteed, but how many will dissent for a 50 will be telling as to how 2027 might evolve.

Not surprisingly, most indicators are oversold. Even if the bulls manage to put up a fight here, the compromised 2700 likely acts as a formidable hurdle.

Tuesday’s spinning top was followed by what looks like a hanging man on Thursday and Friday. These candles are showing up after the US dollar index has rallied in eight of 10 weeks. This week, it rose 0.4 percent to 103.84, where – or between 104 and 105 – dollar bulls will face heavy resistance.

data.title: Stock Market Next Week: Can Stocks And The Euro Fall Further?
data.description:
Can stocks and the euro fall further next week? Yes, and the Fed will not rescue the stock market the way it did in 2019. I expect the Nasdaq 100 to lose another 10% from Friday's close of 25,029, to about 22,500, in the coming weeks, dollar funding strain to keep building, first outside the United States, and the euro to keep falling toward $1.08. Next week's speed depends on Asia's open on Monday: a slow grind below Friday's low of 24,910, toward 24,000, if Asia holds, gaps toward 22,500 if it panics. Rebounds, and history says there will likely be some, are where I would sell again.

This was the Nasdaq 100's worst week since March 2020: it lost 10.43% to 25,028.98, including a 5.61% fall on Friday, and stands 19.8% below its October 6 record. The S&P 500 lost 8.61% to 6,910.39 and chip stocks 17.1%; their index has closed below its 200-day moving average every day since October 30, after 355 sessions above it. The VIX, the implied volatility of the S&P 500 over the next 30 days, went from 19.30 to 35.89, its highest close of the past year. Gold fell 8.9% to $3,538, the 10 year Treasury yield 19 basis points (hundredths of a percentage point) to 4.94%, and the euro closed at $1.0968, a hair above Thursday's closing low of the year.

What I wrote, and what the market did

First, what did not work. On November 6 I called the rebound a dead cat bounce and wrote that a close above 27,270 on the Nasdaq 100 would prove me wrong. It closed at 27,907.63 on November 9, and the fall came a week later than I had written.

On November 14 I wrote: "I don't expect a Santa rally before the Fed meeting of December 9, and if the Fed is still hawkish, there will be no Fed put to support stocks." Since then the S&P 500 has lost 8.6%, and fed funds futures still price a hike on December 9.

The same day, on the euro: "The euro keeps falling against the dollar." It went from $1.1023 to $1.0968. I added: "For EUR/JPY to fall in earnest, USD/JPY has to stop rising." USD/JPY slipped from 159.71 to 158.57, and EUR/JPY fell 1.24% to 173.92, more than against the dollar.

On October 30: "Bonds hedge again, gold does not." This week gold lost 8.9%, to its lowest close of the past year, while the 10 year Treasury yield fell 19 basis points. Stocks and yields now fall together, and gold is sold for cash: a liquidity sell-off, not a flight to safety.

Can the Nasdaq fall another 10%?

Yes. The Nasdaq 100 closed Friday 10.8% below its 200-day moving average of 28,073, the line between a correction in an uptrend and a downtrend. On my Bloomberg, more than half of its members stand at least 20% below their 52-week high. Another 10% would take it to about 22,500, below its March 30 close of 22,953, the low of the past year. Support: Friday's intraday low of 24,910, then 24,000. Resistance: 26,450, between Friday's high and Thursday's close, then 27,000 to 27,600, where it closed from Monday to Wednesday before losing it on Thursday.

What pushes. The sellers come in layers, and none of them has finished.

  • Trend followers (CTAs, funds that buy what rises and sell what falls) are already short: on our terminal, CTA positioning in US equities stood at about minus $20 billion at Friday's close, after flipping from long to short in November.

  • Hedge funds have cut their net bets but not their gross leverage: unwinding it means selling the crowded AI longs. CFTC data for the week to Tuesday, before the worst of the fall, show it: leveraged funds swung by 24,895 contracts to a net short of 10,928 E-mini Nasdaq 100 futures, while covering 68,082 contracts of their short in S&P 500 futures. The bet is against tech, not against the whole market.

  • Volatility-targeting funds (vol control, risk parity) keep their risk constant, so they sell stocks when volatility rises, and bonds too if funding strain lifts yields.

  • Leveraged ETFs, most of them on tech, sell into the close on big down days.

  • Dealers, the market's plumbing, carried about $97 billion of Treasury bills on November 11, in the top fifth of their two-year range. If funding tightens, they quote less, and a correction gaps.

  • Credit now feeds equity. High yield spreads, the extra yield junk bonds pay over Treasuries, widened 51 basis points to 367, and those of the riskiest tier, rated Caa, 91 to 1,174, both one-year highs. CoreWeave's five year credit default swap, the price of insuring its debt, ended at 1,291 basis points, also a one-year high. On Friday CoreWeave lost 12.0%, Nebius 16.1%, Nvidia 14.0% and Oracle 8.5%, and Anthropic, which raised the most money ever for a new share issue (private placement included), lost 8.5% and ended Friday less than $6 above its offering price. The AI buildout is now testing how much money markets can supply: on Thursday SpaceX priced about $32 billion of bonds, arranged by Goldman Sachs and Apollo, through a vehicle that buys Nvidia chips and leases them to SpaceX, and the part sold to corporate bond buyers had to pay about 100 basis points more than SpaceX's own bonds of similar maturity sold earlier this year.

What brakes. Companies buying back their own shares, now out of their blackout, are the largest buyer against the fall. Pension funds rebalance into stocks after a drop, a bid that fades under stress. Asset managers rotate into quality, not the Nasdaq: this week the equal weight S&P 500 lost about 6.2%, against 8.6% for the index and 12.5% for technology stocks, while consumer staples, at a record close on Monday, lost 2.1%. On Thursday my colleague Lucas Erbrech, of the CrossVol Derivatives Team, looked at where to hide if the AI trade breaks. Part of the trend-following selling has already happened. There is no capitulation yet, so the flush that usually ends a fall is still ahead. All these sellers share one circuit breaker: a fall deep enough to exhaust the trend followers and push the Fed to its balance sheet.

Confirmation: a close below 24,910, then 24,000, or another credit event at a neocloud, an AI cloud renter such as CoreWeave or Nebius. Invalidation: a close back above 26,450 that holds, with a Fed that signals a pause in December.

What happens in Asia on Monday?

Asia has to absorb Friday's fall in New York first, and that decides the speed: Tokyo, Seoul and Taipei had closed before it. In New York on Friday, Taiwan Semiconductor's shares lost 9.5%, the Taiwan and Korea ETFs 11.0% and 8.4%, and Nikkei futures in Chicago settled 3.3% below Tokyo's close. Asian investors are still heavily invested in AI and semiconductors. Taiwan's Taiex already lost 17.5% this week, and Taiwan's Financial Supervisory Commission has tightened again after a first round on November 9. From Friday, a stock that closes down 3.5% or more cannot be sold short below its previous close the next day. On Saturday it extended the ban to all listed stocks from Monday, raised the minimum margin on short sales from 130% to 150% and suspended new listings of put warrants.

In Japan, I am wary of SoftBank. Its shares lost 14.5% on Friday to ¥3,025, the lowest close of the past year, 65% below their June 2 high. ARM, the chip designer whose shares back SoftBank's financing, then lost 14.1% in New York after Tokyo had closed. On September 25 I wrote: "The collateral chains are circular. SoftBank's margin loan is secured on ARM shares." That is my weak point to watch: ARM in New York on Monday, then SoftBank on Tuesday, when Tokyo reopens after a public holiday.

So my base case for the week is conditional. If Asia does not panic at the open, I expect a slow, choppy grind lower on the Nasdaq 100, below Friday's low of 24,910 and toward 24,000. If it does panic, the fall goes faster, with gaps, toward my 10%. The first answer comes on Monday at 1:00 a.m. Paris time, when Seoul opens, then Taipei at 2:00. Japan's markets are closed on Monday for Labor Thanksgiving Day, a public holiday, so Tokyo only answers on Tuesday, at the same hour.

Are investors hedging?

Yes, judging by option prices: close to the money and for the next few days. The VVIX, the volatility of the VIX, which rises when investors pay up for VIX calls, went from 101.53 to 138.03, above its November 5 crash level and far above the 121 of October 16. The VIX curve inverted from the short end: 40.72 for the 9-day VIX, 35.89 for the 30-day, 30.94 for the 3-month. The 1-day VIX closed at 51.34, a one standard deviation move of about 3.2% priced for Monday alone.

On my Bloomberg's volatility surface (3:50 p.m. New York time), four week implied volatility on S&P 500 options 1.5% below the index doubled between the two Fridays, from 16.5% to 33.8%, while puts 10% below went from 26.5% to 43.1%, a smaller rise. The Cboe SKEW index, a gauge of how expensive far out of the money puts are, fell every day of the week, from 147.14 to 138.84. And some were still selling volatility: in the week to Tuesday, leveraged funds added 38,154 contracts to their net short in VIX futures, to 72,916, just before the VIX jumped. Investors hedging at the money expect a move, not a collapse. On October 18 I wrote: "The VIX woke up on Friday, and it woke up loaded the other way."

Is there a dollar funding problem?

Not yet in the United States, but it is building outside, and that is the second part of my view. In the US, the plumbing is tight, not broken. The Fed's reverse repo facility, the cushion where money funds parked spare cash, held $0.4 billion on Friday, so every new Treasury bill now draws on bank reserves ($3.0 trillion on Wednesday). SOFR, the main overnight repo rate, printed 3.91% on Thursday, 1 basis point above the 3.90% the Fed pays on reserves, after 3.97% at the start of the month. The Fed's standing repo facility, the emergency door at 4.00%, lent $1 million on Friday, and the swap lines with the ECB and the Bank of Japan are almost unused.

One leveraged position keeps growing: in the week to Tuesday, leveraged funds added 181,116 contracts to their short in 10 year Treasury note futures and 52,916 in ultra long bond futures, while covering 2 and 5 year. That is the futures leg of the basis trade, funded in repo, and it keeps moving to the long end, as I wrote on September 22 in The Basis Trade Did Not Shrink Its Risk. It Moved It to the Long End.

Outside, the strain is visible. I could not read the cross-currency basis, the direct price of borrowing dollars against euros, on Friday (minus 3.6 basis points at the end of October, when I wrote that French stress had reached dollar funding), so I use interbank funding. Three month Euribor, the rate at which banks lend each other euros, closed 23.2 basis points above the three month €STR swap, the expected overnight rate, against 17.5 a week earlier and about 11 in late September. In Tokyo, three month TIBOR stands 46.4 basis points above its overnight swap, against 41.4. In India, the central bank accepted none of the 81 bids at a six month bill auction on November 4; the next two auctions were fully accepted, but one year bills yield 113 basis points above the policy rate. China's factory index fell to 49.3 in October, below the 50 line. Brazil's main stock index closed Thursday 20.4% below its October 9 record (Friday was a holiday there). Foreign central banks' Treasury holdings at the New York Fed fell on November 11 to $2.52 trillion, the lowest since October 2010, and recovered $20 billion a week later.

Signs the squeeze has reached New York: SOFR more than 5 basis points above the effective fed funds rate, weaker Treasury auctions ($183 billion of notes next week), the standing repo facility used in size, and the French spread over Germany back above its October 22 closing peak of 174 basis points (157 on Friday).

Can the euro fall to 1.08?

Yes, I expect it to get there. EUR/USD closed below 1.10 every day this week and ended at $1.0968. Below 1.0950, my next levels are 1.0913, 1.0880 and 1.08.

The rate gap did not push it this week: markets price a 92% chance of a Fed hike on December 9 and 91% for the ECB on December 17, and the two year gap between Treasury and German yields narrowed from 171.6 to 158.8 basis points. What pushes the euro lower is the demand for dollars in a sell-off, and France: its 10 year spread over Germany widened to 157 basis points, it pays 47 more than Italy, and S&P is scheduled to review its rating on Friday. One month implied volatility on EUR/USD is only 6.13%: FX options are still calm.

Positioning is the risk. Speculators held a net short of 142,710 euro futures contracts on Tuesday, November 17. Apart from the two previous reports, of October 27 and November 3, it has not been this large since January 2016.

A crowded short is not a squeeze on its own: it needs a catalyst, and a hawkish ECB on December 17 could be one. My views also have one friction: a US crash deep enough to break the labor market would take the Fed's hike off the table, and with it the dollar's main support. Then the euro would stop around 1.08 to 1.09. My euro call works best in an orderly decline, not in a crash.

Will the Fed rescue stocks like in 2019?

No. The comparison everyone makes this week is the autumn of 2018. On November 20, 2018, the S&P 500 stood 9.9% below its September record. It lost another 11.0% into Christmas Eve, and the rebound held once the Fed turned, in January 2019. This year it closed Friday 11.6% below its October 6 record: a similar distance, in the same season. But on October 13 I also wrote: "That analogue needs a Fed that turns." This Fed has no reason to turn.

In 2018 the Fed could turn at no cost: inflation was at target and growth was slowing. Today core PCE inflation is 3.1%, core consumer prices rise 0.3% a month, and growth runs at 3.4% annualized. The Fed's staff blames tariffs, energy and the AI buildout itself. Cutting now would look like surrender.

The committee says it in its own words. On October 28 it held the federal funds rate at 3.75% to 4.00%, and two members voted for a hike. The minutes, published on Wednesday, say that "almost all participants judged" that further action to raise rates "would likely be appropriate". They also say that almost all participants discussed the risk that "the returns on AI investment turned out to be disappointing to investors". The Fed sees the AI risk and has decided that inflation comes first.

If the sell-off goes on, the repricing runs down one rung at a time. Fed funds futures price 0.92 of a quarter point hike on December 9, against 1.06 a week earlier, when a small chance of a half point was also in the price. The half point is gone. Next comes a pause. A cut needs new information: payrolls that break, oil that falls hard (Brent is at $92.57), a funding accident.

Support, if it comes, will come from the balance sheet: the New York Fed can buy Treasury bills to keep reserves ample (zero in October, decided month by month). That calms repo and short rates, not the Nasdaq.

How far can a rebound go?

History says a rebound is likely, and that in markets this volatile it was more often a chance to sell than the start of a recovery. Since 1985 the Nasdaq 100 has had 30 weeks like this one, a fall of 10% or more over five sessions (counting at most one per month). In 24 of them it was already as volatile as now, with typical daily moves above 2.2% over the previous month (2.4% today). In those 24 episodes:

  • One week later, the index was higher 15 times, by a median of 1.8%.

  • Within two weeks, its best close was at least 5% above the starting point 17 times, and the median best close was 7.0% higher.

  • One month later, it was higher only 13 times (median +0.9%), and below its best close of the first two weeks 15 times, by a median of 5.1 percentage points.

  • Along the way, it closed below the starting level at some point in 18 of the 24 episodes, a median of 6.4% lower.

From Friday's 25,029, a 5% to 7% rebound would take the Nasdaq 100 to about 26,280 to 26,780, into the 26,450 resistance and toward the 27,000 to 27,600 zone it lost on Thursday. A 6.4% fall from Friday would take it to about 23,430.

What could trigger a rebound next week?

This week investors bought puts close to the money, and the dealers who sold them hedged by selling futures. As I explained on November 14 in No Santa Rally Before the Fed, when implied volatility falls those puts lose delta, the hedge becomes too big and dealers buy futures back: a vanna rally. Time does the same over a long weekend. With the 1-day VIX at 51, any session that passes without a shock can start one. The catalysts on the calendar:

  • Monday, Asia's open. If Seoul and Taipei absorb Friday's fall in New York without panic, on the first day of Taiwan's wider short-sale ban, implied volatility can drop fast. That is the first and most likely trigger. Tokyo, closed on Monday for a public holiday, follows on Tuesday. Asia also has its own hawks this week: Bloomberg Economics expects a rate hike in South Korea, and Tokyo inflation that supports a December hike by the Bank of Japan. The US sells 2 year notes the same day (5 year on Tuesday, 7 year on Wednesday, $183 billion in all).

  • Until Saturday, November 28, when the Fed's quiet period before its December 8-9 meeting starts: any Fed official who opens the door to a pause.

  • Wednesday: October PCE inflation, the second estimate of third quarter GDP and jobless claims, a day early. A soft PCE print would trim the 92% chance of a December hike, but it is not the base case: Bloomberg Economics expects headline PCE prices up 0.32% in October, taking the yearly rate to 3.8% from 3.6%.

  • Thursday and Friday: Thanksgiving, US markets are closed on Thursday, early close at 1:00 p.m. New York time on Friday. Over the long weekend short-dated puts lose value on their own. The Thanksgiving week has been positive for the Nasdaq 100 in 27 of the last 40 years, but not in 2018, when it lost 5.0%.

  • Into month end: pension funds rebalancing toward stocks after the fall.

For the euro, S&P's scheduled review of France comes on Friday and Spain's snap election on Sunday. Then euro area inflation on December 1, payrolls on December 4, the Fed on December 9, US CPI on December 10, the ECB and France's budget deadline on December 17, the Bank of Japan on December 18.

How would I use a rebound?

I would not chase the fall from here. I would use the rebounds. A vanna rally that stalls at 26,450, or in the 27,000 to 27,600 zone, is where I would sell the Nasdaq 100 again and buy put spreads (buying a put and selling a lower one to cap the cost). After such a rally implied volatility is lower, so protection costs less, and the index sits under resistance. That is what the history above favors. A bounce is not a reclaim: what would prove me wrong is a close above 26,450 that holds for several sessions, with a Fed that signals a pause in December.

What comes next for me. This week fits the sequence I have followed since September: the AI shock, then credit, then dollar funding. The first two are in the prices. The third is building outside the United States. That systemic phase is the next chapter I will write.

data.title: Why Your Priciest Stocks Fall First
data.description:
Valuation is a put option. A cheap stock holds up better during multiple compression.

Multiple compression means the market pays less for every $1 of earnings. Rising rates and slowing earnings are driving it now.

Sellers go after the priciest stocks first.

You probably lean on the chart or hide in big names that feel safe.

Don’t get me wrong. Charts matter.

Those companies make big money. Yet neither one tells you what you’re paying.

I’ll show you how I check that with the P/E ratio. You only need a calculator and four quarters of earnings.

The P/E only gets you halfway. You also have to read it against its peers.

My $108,000 account lost $1,200 over three days while the S&P 500 fell 300 points. One futures contract on the index would’ve lost $15,000.

Everything I own has a low multiple.

Let’s start with how multiple compression works. Then I’ll show you the check behind every Genesis COG trade.

How Multiple Compression Works

A multiple is the price you pay for every $1 a company earns. Wall Street calls it the P/E.

Declining earnings and rising interest rates set off multiple compression. Investors start paying less for that same $1.

Bull markets need falling rates and faster growth. Stocks are pricing in a slowdown while bond yields price in inflation.

I call that a bad combo. The Fed’s latest minutes show almost every official expects more rate hikes.

The 30-year Treasury pays about 5.5%. A growth stock with no dividend pays you nothing while you wait.

Earnings beats are slowing to a crawl. Sellers are spreading multiple compression across the whole market.

Jeffrey Gundlach won’t consider the S&P 500 until its P/E falls below 15. The bond king is holding about 30% in stocks.

I agree with him. A 15 multiple would be the buy of the century.

Why Multiple Compression Hits The Priciest Stocks First

The higher the multiple, the harder multiple compression hits the stock.

A multiple of 40 gets me out of a stock. I stay calm at 6x because that multiple works as a floor.

Nvidia (NVDA) sat at 40x when multiple compression started hitting it. It’s already broken.

Drug stocks proved it again this week. Merck (MRK) was down $4.75 on Wednesday when it ran out of buyers.

Bristol Myers (BMY) broke too. GlaxoSmithKline (GSK), the cheapest of the group at about 10x, is down only a fraction.

I own GlaxoSmithKline because it’s cheap.

I’d lighten up on Eli Lilly (LLY) first. It added $269 billion in market value since Oct. 6.

Only Apple (AAPL) added more. I have Lilly at 46x earnings, while its peers trade at 10x to 12x.

I know Lilly is making big money. I’d still fire you if you worked for me and paid 46x for it.

I think it’s the one stock that could break this market.

Why A Low Multiple Works Like A Put

A put option gains value when a stock falls. It works like insurance on the shares you own.

A low multiple does the same job during multiple compression. It limits how far a stock can fall.

Each point on an S&P 500 futures contract is worth $50. That 300-point drop cost $15,000 on one contract.

I kept my loss to $1,200 with three habits.

I’m hedged. No position tops 4%.

Every stock I own also carries a low multiple.

Sellers hit the market for a fifth straight day on Thursday. One futures contract was down $5,000 at one point.

I was down $300 on my $108,000 account.

I didn’t always trade this way. I was Mr. Momentum 20 years ago.

I was up 30% one year and lost 30% the next. I blew my accounts out.

I’ve made more mistakes over 38 years than all of you combined.

Valuation is a put option. Everything I buy starts with it.

The Check Behind Every Genesis COG Trade

I run three steps to gauge multiple compression risk before I buy:

  1. Add up four quarters. Total the last four quarters of earnings. Divide that into the share price.

  2. Read it against the peers. Check what similar companies trade for.

  3. Let the chart pick the day. I don’t buy on the way down, no matter how cheap.

Williams-Sonoma (WSM) is a $230 stock. Its last four quarters add up to close to $10.

That’s about 22x earnings. I won’t pay that with housing in a bear market.

That bear market could drag it into multiple compression.

Marvell (MRVL) came out at 45x on a calculator I borrowed from my daughter. The semiconductor I bought that day trades at 11x.

I like my chances of multiple expansion better.

I track about 40 bank stocks. Only Wells Fargo (WFC) trades cheaper than U.S. Bancorp (USB), the one I own.

The chart only tells me when. Value comes first.

Stuff that’s cheap always comes back.

Every Genesis COG trade follows that order.

The model picks the timing only after the value checks out. It never buys in a downward channel.

I’m holding 55% cash right now. I won’t force a trade to put it to work.

data.title: Will There Be Another Government Shutdown This Year?
data.description:
I’d like to see a shutdown or continuing resolution for the rest of the year. But what are the odds?

The above Government Shutdown graph is from Polymarket, with my highlights and arrows.

At times there is little difference between December 12 and December 31. Other times, like now there is a substantial difference between the two dates.

Currently the odds for December 12 are 24 percent. The odds for December 31 are 36 percent.

Key Dates

  • December 11: The current continuing resolution (H.R. 6500 / Public Law 119-103) funds federal agencies through 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on Friday, December 11, 2026. After that moment, the money runs out unless Congress passes (and the President signs) new funding before then.

  • December 17: The last scheduled House session day is December 17, 2026.

  • December 18: The last scheduled Senate session day is December 18, 2026.

  • December 19: Congress leaves for the Christmas/holiday recess. The 119th Congress’s term officially ends. Hooray!!

  • January 3, 2027: 120th Congress convenes at noon on January 3, 2027

The Dec 17-19 are published targets. They can shift if unfinished business (especially the December 11 funding deadline) keeps them in session longer, but the plan is to finish before Christmas and not return until the new Congress begins.

Continuing Resolution

There is no Polymarket contract on another continuing resolution, but this is what would happen.

If Congress passes (and the President signs) another continuing resolution that funds the government through December 31, 2026 (or into early January 2027):

  • There would be no funding lapse on December 12 or later in December. Agencies would keep operating at roughly the current levels.

  • The next deadline would fall after the current (119th) Congress ends. The new 120th Congress — with Democratic majorities in both chambers — takes office at noon on January 3, 2027. Any further funding bill would then be negotiated and passed under the new majority.

  • Pending legislation that doesn’t pass before adjournment generally dies and has to start over.

A short extension past the 11th remains possible, but it doesn’t guarantee funding stays in place through year-end without further action. That is the main reason the “December 31” odds are higher than the “by December 12” odds.

In short, a year-end CR is the classic “kick the can” move. It clears the immediate December cliff but leaves the real spending decisions for the incoming Congress.

Republicans do not want to kick the can here. Yet, they do not have the votes to get what Trump wants.

Why I Support a Shutdown

I would like to see all funding, especially for the war and ICE to be frozen in place until the next Congress. A continuing resolution with no additional funding would also suffice.

Then I want to see funding for ICE totally removed and military spending reduced.

Unfortunately, there is roughly no chance of ICE funding removed and military spending reduced, but the less funding all around for anything, the happier I am.

On the plus side, I do not believe Trump and Hegseth will get all the military funding they seek. Expect Senate compromises for which Thune will get the blame.

Importantly, the harder Hegseth and Trump push for full military funding without offsetting budget cuts, the less likely they get anything.

So let the Republican bickering and infighting continue. The more the better because we are heading into the lamest of lame duck final two years.

data.title: Do Term Spread Inversions Help Predict Australian Recessions?
data.description:
Do term spread inversions help predict Australian recessions? Not really, even using alternative recession chronologies.

Figure 1: Top panel,  Australia10 year-3 month term spread, %, and ECRI defined peak-to-trough recession dates shaded light blue, Middle panel, Light green denotes trough to peak unemployment rate defined dates. Melbourne Institute defined recession dates shaded light violet, Bottom panel, modified Sahm rule peak to trough (+0.75 ppt threshold). Unemployment rate available only starting 1978M02, so no Sahm rule based recession dates before 1979M02; end date is assumed equal to ECRI’s. Source: ECRI, Melbourne Institute, author’s calculations. 

While ECRI and the Melbourne Institute largely agree on the mid-1980’s and 1990-91 recessions, and agree on the no-2009 recession call, they do disagree on the 1970’s recessions.

Interestingly, the Sahm rule (with a 75 bps threshold instead of 50 bps, as suggested by the RBA), would posit a recession in 2001 and 2009. However, total employment as well as GDP do not decline on a sustained basis.

None of these recession are predicted with an pseudo-R2 greater than 0.14 over 1986-26m (the coefficient on the spread is opposite of expected). Restricting the sample to the pre-pandemic period raises the pseudo-R2 to up to 50% for ECRI or Melbourne Institute chronologies; but the spread still retains the “wrong” sign.

Note that the lack of predictive power for recessions is different from lack of predictive power for, say, GDP growth (e.g., Poke, Wells, 2009).

data.title: Disney Produces Mediocre FCF Growth - How To Play DIS After Its Recent Rise
data.description:
The Walt Disney Company (DIS) generated 89% higher FCF in fiscal Q4, ending Oct. 3, but only 4.9% higher for the year. Moreover, in the Nov. 17, 2026, shareholder letter, management guided FCF up just 4% for next year. So, is DIS stock at a peak?

DIS closed down about 1.7% on Friday at $118.11, after rising to a 6-month peak after its results release. Moreover, since its recent low of $101.33 on Oct. 1, DIS stock is up 17.0%.

DIS stock - last 6 months - Barchart - Nov. 20, 2026

Mediocre FCF Growth

FCF for FY 2026 came in at $10.572 billion, just 4.9% higher than the $10.077 billion, as seen on page 11 of its shareholder letter. Moreover, its annual FCF margin fell from 10.67% of revenue last year to 10.33% this year, according to Stock Analysis.

So, since analysts project 4.0% higher revenue in 2027 at $106.52 billion next year, and management is forecasting just $11.0 billion in FCF (i.e., up 4.05%), the FCF margin should stay level at 10.33% next year.

The problem is this mediocre growth rate is already discounted in the stock price after its recent rise. Moreover, analysts and the market want to see better than mediocre FCF growth and higher FCF margins.

DIS Price Targets

Nevertheless, analysts still see DIS stock as undervalued. For example, 32 analysts surveyed by Yahoo! Finance have an average price target (PT) of $131.34. That's about 10.7% higher.

Barchart's mean survey PT is slightly higher at $132.22, and AnaChart's survey of 20 analysts has an average of $132.31. AnaChart's average PT tends to be based on more recent analysts' write-ups. These last 2 PTs are 11.4% higher than its close on Friday.

So, if FCF will only be 5% higher, as management projects, why do these analysts still think there is 10-11% upside left in the stock?

One reason could be that DIS is trading well below its historical average price/earnings (P/E) metric.

For example, Seeking Alpha shows that DIS's forward P/E for the past 5 years has been 21.69x. Analysts' Sept. 2027 $7.57 EPS forecast average puts DIS on a forward P/E of just $15.67x. That implies a 38.4% upside potential (21.69/15.67x-1).

Similarly, Morningstar's 18.9x 5-year historical forward P/E average implies 20.6% upside. The average of these two implies upside of  29.5%.

However, the 5% FCF growth rate provided by management dampens this potential upside. The average of 29.5% and 5.0% is 17.25% upside.

Given a 5% discount rate for one year, the potential upside is just 16.42%, or a PT of $137.34. That is close to where the average of these analysts' price targets are today.

How to Play DIS

Since there may be limited upside, it could make sense for conservative investors to wait for DIS stock to move back down. 

Then the investor can do short-put plays at out-of-the-money (OTM) strike prices, or covered calls if the investor is already a shareholder. Less risk-averse investors can also do short put credit spreads. 

In addition, at that point, some investors might be willing to invest in long-dated in-the-money (ITM) DIS call options.

As a result, some investors may feel it makes sense to wait until there is at least a mid-20% upside potential using several metrics.

data.title: Progress Isn’t Protection
data.description:
This week, Microsoft (MSFT)’s Outlook service went down. A software problem disrupted banking transactions at JPMorgan Chase (JPM) and other major banks. And apparently one router in Arkansas triggered an air traffic control communications failure that brought departures across the country to a halt.

Meanwhile, in China, a battery-powered aircraft designed to carry 19 passengers completed its first flight with a crew aboard.

Extraordinary progress. Surprisingly fragile systems.

Those aren’t contradictory descriptions of the world we live in. They’re increasingly descriptions of the same world.

Consider Equinor (EQNR), the Norwegian energy company. As of Thursday, it was still working to contain a cyberattack. Yet the company’s oil and gas production was running normally, with no indication that data had been stolen or altered.

That’s an important distinction. Resilience doesn’t always mean preventing something from going wrong. Sometimes it means keeping the essential things working while you deal with what went wrong.

The electric aircraft offers a different lesson. China’s CE-25A flew about 37.5 miles with two pilots and a flight-test engineer aboard. It’s an engineering milestone. Just last week, a noted energy analyst told me battery-powered airplanes would never work at scale. This flight doesn’t settle that argument. A successful test and a commercially viable airline service are very different things.

Source: Gulf News

Still, it is worth paying attention to. The fact that it happened in China gives me another reason to reflect on what I saw during my recent visit.

The world is gaining extraordinary capabilities. But as we are learning, adding capabilities and reducing vulnerabilities aren’t necessarily the same thing.

Efficiency Isn’t Resilience

For decades, the global economy rewarded efficiency. The push was to make things wherever they’re cheapest, keep inventories lean, and automate what you can. For the most part, that approach worked.

Spare capacity costs money was the thinking of the day. So do backup suppliers and alternative ways of getting things done. When everything works, those costs are easy to question. When something fails, you discover what they were buying you.

Efficiency and resilience aren’t opposites. A well-run business needs both. The problem comes when we squeeze out every inefficiency without asking whether some of it serves a purpose.

The same question applies to countries. And, as I’ll get to in a moment, to you and me.

Still Connected. More Cautious.

This week’s APEC summit in Shenzhen offers a useful reminder that competing with another country and doing business with it are not mutually exclusive.

Mainstream media focused on Xi Jinping, Donald Trump, and Vladimir Putin sitting at the same table, discussing limits to nuclear weapons.  Those talks were taking place alongside an economic gathering with a different emphasis. At APEC, Xi called for more open trade, closer regional integration, and cooperation in artificial intelligence. I wouldn’t confuse that with an end to strategic competition. Nor would I confuse strategic competition with an end to trade.

The more useful question is where countries are willing to depend on one another—and where they want alternatives.

That’s how I think about resilience. Not complete self-sufficiency, not walking away from every relationship that carries risk. Rather, understanding which dependencies could leave you exposed and deciding what to do about them.

Shenzhen is an unusually good place to think about that question. It was the final stop on my eight-day trip through mainland China’s top-tier cities a few weeks ago.

A recent Bloomberg report describes the city as a showcase for China’s technological ambitions: Huawei, BYD (BYDDF), DJI, robotics, and artificial intelligence. It also describes a less comfortable side of the story—pressure on business profits and workers who aren’t sharing equally in the prosperity.

One parcel delivery worker told Bloomberg his monthly income had fallen from roughly 15,000 yuan a few years ago to about 9,000 yuan. That’s a substantial decline in a city producing some of the world’s most advanced technology.

One worker’s experience isn’t a measure of an entire economy. Nor does it establish that technology caused his pay to fall. But put those two pictures side by side: remarkable industrial capabilities and a household getting by on less.

Technological leadership and household financial security are not the same thing. Which brings up a question: What happens when a country becomes more resilient, but the people living inside it don’t?

Governments and large companies can devote enormous resources to securing supplies, developing alternatives, and protecting essential operations.

Individuals don’t always have that luxury.

The ability to adapt to change looks very different depending on whether you have savings, flexibility, and rising income—or are working harder to cover the same bills. That raises bigger questions about wages, work, and who benefits from technological progress.

There is a narrower question we can do something about today: How much of our financial life depends on everything working exactly as it should?

One phone. One email account. One bank. One copy of an important document.

We can’t control the pace of technological change or the relationship between Washington and Beijing. But we can identify a few points of failure in our own lives, and give ourselves alternatives.

I’m not suggesting you build a bunker, but if the world’s biggest powers are focusing on resilience, what does the same exercise look like for you and me?  

Here’s where I would start.

Protect Your Access

First and foremost, use strong, unique passwords for your important accounts. A password manager makes that much more manageable.

Strong passwords are the starting point, not the whole strategy. Turn on the strongest authentication your provider offers. Where available, phishing-resistant options such as security keys provide stronger protection than relying on a password alone.

Then learn how account recovery works. I can tell you from firsthand experience: The time to figure out how to regain control of an important account is well before you lose access. Once you are locked out, you are operating from a position of weakness. Not fun.

Keep recovery codes somewhere secure that you can reach even if your phone is unavailable. Think through the obvious question: If my phone disappeared tomorrow, how would I get back in?

Protect your phone number, too. Ask your carrier how to block unauthorized SIM changes and transfers of your number to another carrier. These aren’t necessarily the same setting. Verizon (VZ) and AT&T (T) both offer SIM Protection and Number Lock features.

And give your wireless account the same attention you give your financial accounts.  Using a lame password to protect your wireless account is an invitation to a world of trouble.

Keep Your Own Records

Download your financial institutions’ monthly statements, including holdings and share counts—not just a screenshot of the balance.

Keep copies of your insurance policies and other important documents somewhere you can reach them if your usual account or device is unavailable.

The key is not to create another single point of failure.

A copy on the laptop next to you isn’t much help if both copies disappear with the laptop. And an external drive attached to your computer is not an offline backup.

Keep a secure backup somewhere other than your house. At least one backup should also be disconnected from your computer when it isn’t being updated. Occasionally check that you can actually restore the files. A backup and process that you’ve never tested is an assumption, not a plan.

Have an Alternative

Governments and large companies often maintain more than one supplier. Consider applying that same thinking to your financial life.

If your day-to-day banking runs through one institution, a second banking relationship may be worth considering. The point isn’t to predict which bank might have a problem. It’s to avoid having every option depend on the same system.

Have some cash on hand.  In our increasingly cashless society, a stash of $20s can get you out of a short-term jam, be it cyber, weather, or institutional in nature.

Review your insurance with the same mindset. Ask what is covered, what is excluded, and where you may be assuming protection you don’t actually have.  For example, do you have cyber coverage, and if not, should you? Don’t wait until it’s too late to find out.

Make a Family Plan

Precautions are less useful if only one person in the household knows how they work.

Make sure your spouse or another trusted person knows where to find essential information and what to do if you’re unavailable.

Have a safe word or phrase that you, your spouse, and your kids know but never share.  Don’t email it to each other.  Set the safe word in person.  This is a way to verify identity if you get an unexpected request for money. Its purpose is to give everyone permission to pause and verify, rather than act under pressure. Keep the plan simple enough that your family will remember it when they’re worried or distracted.

A Little Preparation Goes a Long Way

The goal here isn’t to anticipate every possible failure. It’s to make sure one failure doesn’t become five.

I’m enthusiastic about what technology can do. What I saw in China gave me plenty to think about. I expect the coming years to bring advances that improve our lives in ways we haven’t yet imagined. I also expect the advances to come at us more and more quickly, and that can cause problems.
