data.title: Kroger Lays Off American Workers, Moves Jobs To India
data.description:
Kroger (KR) has started laying off about 3,000 American white-collar workers at the same time it’s developing an operations center in India that is hiring dozens of workers.

That puts the company, which has described itself as “America’s favorite grocer,” at odds with how most Americans feel about U.S. jobs being outsourced overseas.  

“Overall, when Americans are asked what hurts American workers, the top answers are outsourcing jobs to other countries (80% of Americans think this hurts U.S. jobholders), more foreign-made products being sold in the U.S. (77% think this hurts), increased use of contract or temporary employees (57%), automation of jobs (50%) and the decline in union membership (49%),” a 2016 Pew Research poll showed.

Kroger has already started notifying workers at its Cincinnati headquarters. It will also be making cuts in other cities where it maintains corporate offices, according to the Cincinnati Business Courier.

And while the cuts have already begun, the company has not shared a timetable for when the full 3,000 would be let go.

The company has, however, moved forward with its plans to launch an operations center in Bangalore, India, and has begun hiring workers there.

A request to Kroger Investor Relations to comment on this story was not immediately returned.

Kroger makes a risky move

While sending jobs to India will help Kroger CEO Gregory Foran’s plan to slash $5 billion in costs from the company that it plans to invest in lower prices, it’s a move that risks alienating customers.

A research paper co-authored by Wharton marketing professor Stefano Puntoni “finds that consumers react far more negatively when layoffs are caused by offshoring. In other words, sending jobs abroad does not just affect the workers — it dents the company’s image, too.”

The paper’s key point is based around what the researchers call the “social contract” — the unspoken expectation that firms should support the communities they operate in.

“When a company cuts domestic jobs and moves them overseas, consumers often view it as a betrayal of that norm — even if the move makes business sense on paper,” Knowledge at Wharton shared.

That’s something Puntoni talked about in an interview with Wharton Business Daily.

“We found significantly more negative conversations about collective layoffs when they were about offshoring than about automation,” he said.

Kroger begins outsourcing jobs

Foran has talked about the new facility, but he didn’t actually mention where it was during his comments in Kroger’s fourth-quarter earnings call.

“To support our modernization efforts, we are launching the Kroger Global Capability Center. This initiative is designed to streamline decision-making, improve productivity, and increase the speed at which we execute on behalf of our customers,” he said.

The Kroger CEO focused on the work that would be done at the facility without mentioning that it would be located offshore.

“It complements the work already underway across the organization to modernize how we operate. Work has started and is progressing with speed. We expect modest benefits in 2026 with more significant benefits expected in 2027 and 2028,” he added.

What is the Kroger Capability Center hiring for?

The website talent500.com shows nearly 30 job titles, all in Bangalore, the capital of India’s southern state of Karnataka. LinkedIn also has similar listings, the Cincinnati Business Courier first reported.

The positions include senior real estate portfolio specialist, senior audit analyst, supply chain analyst, lead financial analyst, and logistics operations specialist.

One job listing is looking for a “Manager, Supply Chain Analytics” and requires 7-11 years of experience. The description makes it clear that it’s a high-level position.

“Lead advanced supply chain analytics and modeling that support network strategy, flow strategy, capacity planning, and strategic decision-making. Own the repeatable data foundation, models, dashboards, and scenario analysis needed to evaluate cost, service, capacity, inventory, and operational trade-offs,” the site shared.

Kroger does not list a salary range, but Payscale shows similar jobs in the region averaging 2.8 million rupees, or about $29,500 a year.

In Cincinnati, Payscale shows that an experienced supply chain manager’s median base is $99k, with the 90th percentile at $131,000.

Kroger walks a risky road

While it’s fairly common for large American technology companies to offshore some of their employees, it feels a little different when it’s being done by a grocery chain serving local U.S. neighborhoods.

Microsoft (MSFT) and Apple (AAPL), for example, have a global product, and it makes sense for them to operate in offices around the world.

Kroger, however, only operates in the U.S. The chain has 2,697 stores in 35 states and the District of Columbia.

But it’s also worth noting that Kroger has little choice when it comes to making cuts, according to retail expert Brittain Ladd.

“The layoffs are happening because Kroger’s cost structure has been under pressure for years. The company deferred decisions on outsourcing and technology that many of its competitors made a decade ago, and those decisions are now being made under CEO Greg Foran,” he posted on his LinkedIn page.

Ladd did not comment on the offshoring, but made it clear the company needed to lower its costs.

“As a former consultant to Kroger, I believe the company has little choice but to transform. Maintaining the status quo is not an option,” he wrote.

data.title: Tria and Noah Bring Bank Transfers Directly to Self-Custodial Wallets With Automatic EUR-to-USDC Conversion
data.description:
New York, New York, November 18th, 2026, Chainwire


Powered by Noah's regulated payments infrastructure, Tria's new Currency Accounts let eligible users send euros from their bank and receive USDC in their self-custodial Tria Wallet, usually within minutes, without a crypto exchange or card-based on-ramp.

Tria, the self-custodial neofinance platform, today announced the rollout of Currency Accounts, a new funding capability powered by regulated payments infrastructure provider Noah that connects traditional bank transfers directly to self-custodial wallets through automatic EUR-to-USDC conversion.

After completing a one-time identity check, eligible users receive personal EUR account details, including an IBAN, inside the Tria app. They can then send euros through a standard SEPA bank transfer and receive USDC directly in their self-custodial wallet, usually within minutes. SWIFT transfers are also supported.

The process eliminates the need to first deposit funds on a centralized crypto exchange, purchase digital assets with a card or complete a separate conversion. Noah handles the underlying banking, foreign exchange and compliance infrastructure, while Tria provides the self-custodial wallet where users receive and manage their funds. Tria does not hold users' euros as a bank balance; incoming funds are automatically converted to USDC and delivered to their wallets.

"People shouldn't need an exchange account or a series of transactions just to move money from their bank into a wallet they control," said Vijit Katta, CEO and co-founder of Tria. "We're making that process as familiar as a standard bank transfer. You send euros from your bank, and USDC arrives in Tria, ready to use. That's a significant improvement in how people access onchain finance."
"Moving money into a stablecoin wallet should be as simple as sending a message,” said Shah Ramezani, founder and CEO at Noah. “Noah makes the banking, FX and compliance invisible, so a Tria user simply sends euros and USDC arrives. That's what regulated payments infrastructure should do: take complexity away from the user and simplify stablecoin on ramps.”

The launch gives European users a direct route from their existing bank accounts into Tria's financial ecosystem, including its spending and trading capabilities. It also simplifies access for freelancers, people receiving euro-denominated payments and users who want to move money onchain without relying on a centralized exchange. A Tria Card is not required.

EUR is Tria's first supported fiat currency, with additional currencies planned. The new capability currently supports incoming transfers only; EUR withdrawals to bank accounts are not available through this feature.

Access is rolling out gradually and is expected to reach the full eligible user base over approximately two weeks.

Tria is a self-custodial neofinance platform bringing spending, trading and digital asset management into a unified financial experience. data.description:
I’ve been really dreading this. Global de-risking/deleveraging turned much more serious this week. The AI/tech implosion took a turn for the worse, while cross-asset position liquidations intensified. The leveraged speculating community has suddenly found itself under the most intense pressure since the pandemic. In short, Crisis Dynamics have been unleashed – and I doubt they will be easily contained.

From the deflating historic global Bubbles analytical perspective, this week appeared decisive. It was an especially ominous end to a troubling week.

But at least Wall Street got its beloved Anthropic IPO sold – a suitably grand punctuation mark for history’s greatest era of excess and wealth redistribution. It was also a quick $91 billion liquidity suck for a deleveraging backdrop facing mounting liquidity risk.

From a market instability perspective, it was the worst week since (at least) “liberation day.” The major difference being this week’s turbulence was not triggered by ill-conceived tariff policies, with the President enjoying the ability to easily reverse market sentiment (“Trump put”).

The MAG7 index dropped 5.2% Friday and sank 10.3% for the week, slightly less than the 10.4% “liberation day” weekly loss. Friday losses included Nvidia (NVDA) 14.0%, Tesla (TSLA) 7.6%, Meta 5.9%, and Amazon.com (AMZN) 4.1%. Losses for the week: Nvidia 22.9% (“largest loss since 2008”), Meta 12.6%, Tesla 11.4%, Alphabet (GOOGL) 10.3%, Microsoft (MSFT) 7.5%, Amazon.com 7.4%, and Apple (AAPL) 3.9%. Nvidia CDS surged an unprecedented 22 Friday to a record 145 bps.

Oracle’s (ORCL) 8.5% Friday loss pushed the week’s drop to an alarming 19.3% (down 48% y-t-d). Oracle (’36) yields jumped another 21 bps to 8.31%, with spreads to Treasuries widening 41 bps to a record 337 bps. Oracle CDS jumped 21 Friday to a record 341 bps, with an alarming weekly surge of 42 bps. CoreWeave (CRWV) yields surged 84 bps this week to 15.11%. SpaceX (’36) yields rose 10 bps this week to a record 7.76% (spreads widening 31bps). SpaceX CDS surged 29 this week to 289 bps (almost doubling since early September).

“Risk off” was a global phenomenon. Japan’s Nikkei 225 Index suffered Friday and weekly losses of 5.1% and 7.7% (SoftBank down 14.5% Friday). South Korea’s KOSPI sank 5.2% and 8.0%, ending Friday 48% below the June 19th record high.

The Taiwan TAIEX Index’s 6.2 % Friday loss pushed the week’s slump to a notable 17.5% (“worst week since 1991”) – with the index down 28% from the October 7th high. The Shanghai Composite lost 1.2% Friday (2.8% for the week), with the index down 17% from the May high. Losses were much larger for more tech centric indices. China’s growth-oriented ChiNext Index sank 3.5% Friday and fell 8.8% this week (down almost 50% from June high). Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell 1.9% Friday and 5.2% for the week (down 20% from January high).

Importantly, fear was anything but confined to technology stocks. Ominously, the KBW Bank Index sank 9.5% this week, and the Broker/Dealer Index was hammered 10.4%. Friday losses included Morgan Stanley (MS) (5.3%), Citigroup (C) (4.0%), Bank of America (BAC) (3.2%) and JPMorgan (3.0%). It’s kind of headed in the wrong direction, and it’s spreading out… If you really want to get it down, you’ve got to start taking more aggressive actions.’ ‘You might need to, like, shock people,’ he said.”

History’s greatest Bubble was always going to end badly. It just went on for so long and to such outrageous extremes. Reckless monetary inflation; egregious speculation and leverage; epic malinvestment; deplorable wealth inequality and corruption. And we’ve reached the point where trust in government and our institutions is at such a low ebb. I can’t imagine a more precarious environment for managing financial, economic, social and geopolitical crises.

The unfolding crisis will present a major test for the “Fed put.” Speculative deleveraging will require another major inflation in the Federal Reserve balance sheet. They don’t expect to have to do it; they seemingly don’t have a plan to do it; but they will have no choice.

I come back to the same two questions: Will they move swiftly and in significant size to stabilize markets and restore confidence before things spiral out of control? Understandably, their current focus is to raise rates and get inflation under control. data.title: Gold Extends Decline As Rate Hike Expectations Weigh On Prices
data.description:
Gold (XAU/USD) continues to fall as expectations for further Fed tightening weigh on prices. The break below key weekly support adds to the risk of further declines. The upcoming PCE inflation report could shape interest rate expectations. Stronger inflation may increase pressure on gold, while softer data could support a recovery. Gold also needs to regain its former support area to improve its technical outlook.

Gold under Pressure Ahead of Key PCE Inflation Report

Gold continues to move lower as expectations for further Fed tightening offset the benefit of falling oil prices. WTI crude has lost more than 20% in November, while gold has declined about 8%. Lower energy costs have therefore provided little relief. Tariffs and rising technology costs may keep underlying inflation elevated even as cheaper oil reduces energy expenses. Persistent inflation keeps the focus on interest rates. Higher rates increase the opportunity cost of owning gold because it pays no interest. A stronger dollar also raises its cost in other currencies.

October meeting minutes showed that some Fed officials would consider a larger December increase if inflation data deteriorated. Christopher Waller also raised the possibility of a half percentage point increase or faster subsequent tightening. These messages support the dollar and limit gold recoveries.

The BEA will release October PCE inflation data on November 25. A monthly core reading above the expected 0.3% could support expectations for December and January rate increases. A reading of 0.1% or less could reduce those expectations and support gold. Preliminary November business surveys will also influence the dollar. If Fed officials push back against faster rate increases, gold could find additional support.

Gold Breaks below Weekly Descending Triangle Support

The gold chart below shows a descending triangle with a falling upper boundary and a horizontal base around $3,850 to $4,000. Gold failed to remain above this support area and continued to move lower. The red circle marks the final recovery attempt near the triangle floor. The large weekly decline extends below the former support range. This breakdown shifts attention toward lower historical support levels.

The $3,500 area provides the first nearby reference. Below it, the dashed horizontal support lies near $3,450. This line marks a previous price ceiling before the earlier advance accelerated. A test could slow the decline, but gold needs to establish a base to signal stability. A sustained move below $3,450 would expose the former consolidation area around $3,200 to $3,400. A stable base around these levels could support a recovery, while further declines would keep the outlook negative.

Any recovery initially faces resistance around $3,850 to $4,000. Gold must regain this former support area and remain above it to weaken the breakdown signal. The falling trendline marks the next resistance area as it slopes toward $4,200. A sustained move above that boundary would provide stronger evidence of a trend change. Until then, recoveries may remain vulnerable to renewed declines.

Gold Outlook: Downside Risks Persist Ahead of PCE Inflation

Gold retains a negative outlook as Fed tightening expectations and the weekly triangle breakdown point in the same direction. The immediate downside references are $3,500 and approximately $3,450. Stronger inflation could increase pressure on these levels. Softer data may support a recovery, but lasting technical improvement requires gold to reclaim $3,850 to $4,000. The response to PCE inflation will help determine whether the decline extends or begins to stabilize.

data.title: Gold & Silver Well-Undervalued; S&P Still Way-Overvalued
data.description:
‘Tis hardly the happiest anniversary given the state of the precious metals, but ’twas 17 years ago to this very day (Saturday, 21 November, 2009) that we penned the first edition of The Gold Update in the form of an e-mail to but one recipient … and you know who you are out there, JGS! Now, fast forward with the “eights are wild” as straightway we get into Edition No. 888.

And “oh goodness gracious” are Gold and Silver both so attractively undervalued! It brings to mind such time-honoured expressions as “Time to back up the truck!” and “I love it when I buy Gold and then the price goes down because it’s like having an insurance policy with declining premiums!”

“Well that’s all clever, mmb, but gold and silver are taking a heckova beating…”

Comparatively, Squire, from their respective All-Time Highs (both of which printed back on 29 January), Gold then 5586 settled this past week yesterday (Friday) at 3539, a -37% decline from that top. But poor ol’ Sister Silver — her week’s settle at 41.08 being down from her record 121.78 level — is a fallout of -66%. That acknowledged, regular readers will recall week-in and week-out this past winter our cautioning over the precious metals’ excessively lofty valuations. To wit, our present perspective per the opening Gold Scoreboard:

  • Gold today at 3539 is -14.3% below its Fair Value of 4128;

  • Silver today at 41.08 is -31.3% below its Fair Value of 59.61.

“Got Value?” Hardly does the S&P 500. To be sure, its high-to-low correction thus far is -12.3%. For those of you scoring at home, ’tis — on a mutually discrete basis — the seventh such correction, or worse, thus far this century. But here’s the crazy bit: even now at 6910, the S&P is actually more overvalued today than ’twas on 28 August at 7712. How can that be? Lack of earnings, as in the wrap you’ll see.

“Wow, that is nutz, mmb! But for gold, is this a repeat of 2011-2015?”

Squire, of course, is referring to Gold’s great -46% four-year demise from its then All-Time High of 1923 on 06 September 2011 through the 1045 low of 03 December 2015. And “NO“, dear Squire, ’tis not a repeat. Back then, you’ll recall the world was all “a-ga-ga” (technical term) over the go-go stock market, the S&P soaring 80% for that stint, Gold in turn being once and forevermore discarded as a yieldless, antiquated relic from prior millennia.

But five years hence came COVID combined with the withering of purchasing power via Dollar debasement, the wokey word “awareness” thus returning to Gold, indeed overly so as we witnessed this past winter. Yes, Gold and Silver have taking a hit; but they remain a vastly larger part of the investment conversation today than they did from 2011 through 2015. And reversion in this case back up to their respective valuation means is inevitably in the cards.

All that said, as herein graphically depicted a week ago (and then again emphasized in last Wednesday’s Prescient Commentary), upon Gold’s being unable to regain “The Floor” of 4000, there was “nothing but air” should 3800 fail, all the way down to at least the 3400s, which nearly is what has happened, price on Friday reaching 3503 as the week’s low. And thus, to Gold’s weekly bars and parabolic trends, we go with the 3400-3100 support zone embellished in rose:

‘Course, aiding and abetting the selling of Gold is nervousness of an (albeit improbable) Federal Open Market Committee vote to hike its Bank’s funds rate by +50bp rather than +25bp come the 09 December Policy Statement: certainly Fed Governor and FOMC voting member Christopher “Up the Wall” Waller is in that +50bp camp (as too we herein opined following the Committee’s failure to raise the rate by +25bp back on 28 October).

In fact, next week brings the completion of the October inflation puzzle with the release on Wednesday of the “Fed-favoured” Personal Consumption Expenditures Index, the key “core” rate for which is expected to maintain a +0.3% pace (i.e. +3.6% annualized), nearly double the Fed’s +2.0% desire. And — although oft immaterially — Fed rate hikes may actually decrease the money supply (“M2” basis) as banks pay back debt through the Fed window, which in turn can serve to reduce Gold’s Fair Value. But then again, we reprise this graphic reminder of Gold and the Fed Funds rate from 2004 through 2006: what’s not to like?

Either way, with but 27 trading days remaining in 2026 and Gold now -18.3% from 2025’s settle at 4332, the yellow metal may well be en route to recording a down year, after having on 29 January reached 5586 via our almost perfectly projected high of 5546 … but our forecast low was only 4136, which quite obviously has failed.

Far more overcooked on the downside is the white metal, now -42.1% for 2026. In turn, the Gold/Silver ratio has catapulted from just 46.1x on 27 January to now the year’s high (thus far) at 86.1x. The interpretation? Silver relative to Gold is a STEAL! Reverting merely to the ratio’s evolving mean of 69.3x puts Silver +20% higher from here to 51.10. Indeed should the precious metals record a positive track in 2027, Silver may be next year’s stellar star. To reprise ad nauseam: “Do NOT forget the Silver!!”

That harkened, ’tis a rather sad segue to our two-panel display for Gold’s daily bars from three-months ago-to-date on the left and those for Silver on the right. The baby blue dots of day-to-day trend consistency are erratic at best, and have not led to higher prices (otherwise overwhelmingly the rule rather than this exception) upon passing back up through their respective -80% axes. However, not to worry: our two bawling metals shall get over it once the investing world wakes up to their very attractive undervaluation as aforementioned:

Too, as we go to the 10-day Market Profiles for Gold (below left) and for Silver (below right), they’re akin to those of a week ago, the difference being the pricing scales having both significantly shifted lower. Basement dwellers they are, our precious metals!

Now to the Economic Barometer, which, too, has entered a rather sad state. Of the past week’s 16 incoming metrics, 13 were worse period-over-period, notably including shrinkage in both October’s Leading (aka “lagging”) Economic Indicators and Industrial Production. Also, the pace of Pending Home Sales again retreated. And as stated, the Fed is poised for likely only a +25bp rate hike. Do we dare therefore again mention the “s” word: stagflation? Next week’s mix of nine metrics would “by consensus” appear to be net neutral … but enough so as to curtail the correcting S&P? We shall see by Thursday’s StateSide day of the turkeys… Meanwhile, always heed what the infallible Sibyl sees:

So per our title and analysis, just as Gold and Silver are now well-undervalued, the S&P 500 — even in having so far corrected -12.5% — remains way-overvalued.

The mighty Index stands today at 6910, a level first achieved on 28 October 2025 (269 trading days ago). From there, it took 235 trading days to reach this past 06 October’s record high of 7844 … (deep breath) … only to now have given back the entirety of that gain in just the past 33 trading days. Effectively, that’s a drop at seven times the pace of the overall advance. (Welcome to real markets).

Moreover, we just made the above quip that the S&P today at 6910 is more overvalued than when it was higher on 28 August at 7712. Impossible, right? Wrong. (We purposely selected 28 August as it followed the earnings release of CrowdStrike [CRWD], so as to maintain calculation continuity for the price/earnings ratio of the S&P).

Here you go: the P/E of the S&P at close (7712) on 28 August was 61.5x (or ex-CRWD 38.8x); now, including yesterday’s S&P -3.7% move to 6910, the P/E is actually up to 63.5x (or ex-CRWD 40.0x). Thus from 28 August, the S&P is now -10% lower … but its P/E is +3% higher. What that means for you WestPalmBeachers down there is that by proper earnings valuation, the S&P is even more expensive today than ’twas prior to this correction, (or “crash” as the more ignorant FinMedia outlets are characterizing it).

Further, we acknowledge with Q3 Earnings Season having concluded yesterday, there were year-over-year quarterly improvements for 79% of the S&P 500’s constituents, handily beating the 10-year average (ex-COVID) for improvement of 69%. That’s the good news. But at the risk of being repetitive, the bad news remains the overall paltry level of earnings generation, which is why the P/E is so unsustainably high at 63.5x (or ex-CRWD 40.0x). Recall Jerome B. Cohen’s 15x-18x deemed as “average” for a bull market: we’re double to triple that today, with a one-year U.S. T-Bill market yield four times that of the S&P 500; (but that’s boring).

As to how low the S&P may go: -10% corrections have a hankering of bringing buyers back into the market. And as ’tis that “festive time of year” oft featuring the “Santa Claus Rally”, perhaps stocks now get a grip. But as is our wont, we did a little downside Fibonacci math based on the S&P’s structural correction from last February/March: therein, “Golden Ratio” retracements would be to both 6740 and 6579, that overall structure becoming bust below 6317 (at which from the 7744 record high would then be an all-in correction of some -18% vs. -12% so far). Perhaps not immediately … but then comes January.

Thus, although in correction, ’tis still the way-overvalued S&P…

… as opposed to well-undervalued Gold and Silver!

data.title: The 200-Day Average Broke. The Next 4 Weeks Are Critical
data.description:
The S&P 500 lost 8.6% this week and closed 6% below its 200-day average. Earnings haven’t cracked, which makes this a liquidity event. The question is whether the Fed blinks before the break hardens.

Key Insights

  1. The break below the 200-day average is no longer marginal. The S&P 500 closed at 6,910 on November 20, 6.0% under the average at 7,349, after seven straight losing sessions.

  2. Most first breaks still heal within a month. Since 1950, 18 of the 34 first closes below the 200-day average after a 150-day run above it were back above the line four weeks later.

  3. The deep ones didn’t. All 8 breaks that ran 2.9% or more below the average within their first four sessions were still below it at week four. This one reached 6.0% in four

🏛️ Market Brief – Liquidation, Not A Crash

Last week, in VIX Spike: Complacency’s Bill Coming Due, we warned that low volatility eventually begets high volatility. That bill came due early. The S&P 500 fell 8.6% to 6,910, its seventh straight losing session and the longest losing streak since February 2020. The Nasdaq-100 dropped 10.4%, the Dow lost 8.0%, and the Russell 2000 slid 7.5%. At 11.6% below its October 6 record, the index is in “correction” territory, and the VIX nearly doubled to 37.

So was this a liquidation of leveraged positions due to margin calls? Partly, but not the way the headlines suggest. FINRA’s latest data put margin debt at $1.45 trillion in October, down 2.1% from September and 3.6% below June’s record. Margin borrowing was already easing before the week began.

What we saw instead was mechanical deleveraging. On Thursday, just 38 S&P 500 stocks rose while 464 fell, and all 11 sectors finished lower, even staples. Goldman’s Rich Privorotsky called it “a pretty violent liquidation” in a note covered by ZeroHedge. Dealers were heavily short gamma into Friday’s monthly options expiration, which fed the afternoon selling. Desk chatter also had investors selling gold, copper, crypto and Nvidia (NVDA) to fund allocations in Anthropic’s IPO, which priced at $83 on Wednesday. Gold fell 9.5%, copper 10.2% and Bitcoin (BTC.X) broke below $60,000.

Macro supplied the trigger. Fed Governor Christopher Waller called for a 50-basis-point hike at the December 8-9 meeting after a third straight 0.3% monthly gain in core CPI. The Commerce Department’s rule restricting remote access to advanced AI chips by Chinese firms took effect on Thursday, landing on the AI supply chain the same day. Meanwhile, the 10-year Treasury yield fell to 4.91% from 5.15%. The bond market is starting to price a growth problem, while the Fed is still fighting an inflation problem.

Here is the real question that needs an answer. “Have the fundamentals changed?” Not yet. Through FactSet’s November 13 update, analysts had raised fourth-quarter EPS estimates 1.1% since September 30, something that rarely happens mid-quarter, and third-quarter earnings grew 31.9%.

The Atlanta Fed’s GDPNow still tracks fourth-quarter growth at 3.4%, and initial jobless claims of 203,000 remain near historic lows. Cracks are showing only at the edges. The Philadelphia Fed index collapsed to 6.3 against expectations of 20, the Conference Board’s leading index fell 0.3%, and existing home sales hit their slowest pace since 2010. So far, this is a valuation and liquidity event, not an earnings recession. At 6,910, the S&P 500 trades near 16.6 times FactSet’s November 5 forward earnings estimate of $415.82, down from 17.7 times on that date.

This suggests that the liquidation of positions is likely “overdone.” Since 1950, the S&P 500 has suffered 17 separate episodes in which it fell 8% or more over five sessions. It was higher three months later in 15 of them, with a median gain of 8.1%. The catch is that the median further drawdown along the way was 4.5%, so the bottom rarely arrives on schedule.

Next week, the main focus will be on the Federal Reserve. If Wednesday’s PCE data cools and Fed speakers soften, the setup for a reflexive rally is in place. If not, Privorotsky’s 2018 comparison, when the Fed kept hiking and stocks didn’t bottom until Christmas Eve, becomes the playbook.

📈Technical Backdrop – Oversold, Not Yet Repaired

The S&P 500 closed Friday, November 20, at 6,910.39, down 8.6% for the week. That leaves the index 6.0% below its 200-day average at 7,348.58 and 9.4% below its 50-day average at 7,625.25. It closed below the lower 2-standard-deviation Bollinger Band at 7,094. It also finished just 18 points above the lower 3-SD band at 6,892. To wit: the index ended the week 2.9 standard deviations below its 20-day mean.

The technical backdrop is telling a more interesting story. First, momentum is confirming the extreme selling pressure this past week. On Friday, the 14-day RSI fell to 24.7. That is its lowest reading since April 8, 2025. That date is important as it marked the bottom of the tariff-driven selloff. Notably, during that selloff, the market was being priced for an impact on earnings growth from tariffs. However, currently, analysts continue to maintain or raise earnings estimates for the fourth quarter and next year.

Secondly, the MACD sits at −130 index points, well below its signal line at −75, and Williams %R is at −97. Such is what a forced-selling week looks like on a chart. Oversold is a condition, not a buy signal, and it can persist longer than anyone expects during a liquidation.

Third, breadth tells a more nuanced story. The equal-weight S&P 500 fell 6.1% against 8.4% for the cap-weighted S&P 500 index. The damage has been largely concentrated in the AI complex, with Technology falling 12.3%. However,  semiconductors (SMH) dropped 17.8%, while Nvidia lost 22.9%.

Even the more defensive sectors couldn’t avoid the selling pressure. Staples and Utilities lost 2.0% and 3.0%, respectively. In other words, defensive stocks did their job of reducing the volatility, but they didn’t avoid it. The average stock is in better shape than the index, which helps any rebound broaden. But leadership is what broke, and leadership rarely heals in a week.

Volatility and bonds tell you what kind of selloff this is. The VIX closed at 37.24, nearly double last Friday’s 19.30. Meanwhile, the 10-year Treasury yield fell 24 basis points, and the long-bond ETF (TLT) gained 2.6% while nearly everything else fell. When bonds rally as stocks drop, investors are running from risk rather than scrambling for cash. Watch that relationship next week. If Treasuries start selling off alongside stocks, the liquidation has moved into a more dangerous phase.

In our portfolios, we used the decline to nibble on NVDA and PANW this week. However, these were very small additions, and something that we will likely continue to do into further weakness. Notably, these are NOT calls that the market has bottomed. Next week, we’ll trim value positions to raise cash. That keeps the dip buys from adding to overall equity exposure while the index sits below a level that matters this much. Our 7,000 risk line gave way on Friday, and we’re treating it that way.

For more aggressive traders, the playbook is to let the rubber band snap before acting. With the market at a 2.9-standard deviation (SD) extreme, a reflexive rally toward the lower 2-SD band near 7,094 should be expected. That is a tradeable reflex rally, but should be treated as a strict trade with defined exits.

The 200-day average at 7,349 is the first real test above the market currently. For now, use any rallies into that zone to rebalance and reduce risk rather than chase. However, on the downside, the 3-SD band at 6,892 is only a thin level of support. Any decisive break opens the April 7 close of 6,617, where the spring rally launched.

Next week, there is only one market level that really matters: 7,349. Any snapback toward the 200-day average would be normal from an oversold extreme this deep. What matters is whether the index can close and hold above it. That action will decide whether this break joins the healed ones or the deep breaks that keep going.

🔑 Key Catalysts Next Week

This coming week, Thanksgiving will compress everything into just three trading sessions. Markets are closed on Thursday, and then the market will close early at 1:00 p.m. ET on Friday. For investors, this is a week to turn off monitors and enjoy your family, as the thin holiday trading tends to magnify moves in both directions. With the VIX sitting at 37, this is where investors tend to make mistakes.

The dominant narrative is the Fed. Wednesday brings October personal income and spending. Economists expect core PCE to rise 0.3% for the month and 3.2% from a year ago. A hot print pushes the December debate from 25 basis points toward Waller’s 50. A soft one gives the doves cover. Futures already price in roughly a quarter-point December hike, so the debate is over size, not direction.

The Beige Book follows that afternoon, and New York Fed President John Williams speaks on Monday afternoon. As vice chair of the FOMC, Williams carries more weight than most. He pushed back on a half-point December hike on Tuesday, November 17. Any further sign of flexibility would land hard.

The second narrative is growth. Monday’s flash PMIs and Tuesday’s consumer confidence (expected at 92) will show whether the Philadelphia Fed’s collapse was a one-off. Wednesday also delivers the second estimate of third-quarter GDP, expected at 3.5%. Durable goods orders and weekly jobless claims are released on the same morning, with claims moved up a day due to the holiday.

Two wildcards sit outside the calendar. Anthropic fell 13% in its second session on Friday, according to Bloomberg, and how the largest IPO in history trades in its first full week will color AI sentiment into year-end. Geopolitics is the other. Wolfe Research’s Chris Senyek told Bloomberg that the absence of an Iran peace deal remains an overhang, alongside inflation and AI worries. Neither shows up on a release schedule. Both can move the tape in a holiday-thinned market.

Earnings slow to a trickle, but the names that report matter for the AI debate. Dell (DELL) and Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) offer a direct read on AI server demand after the new chip-access rules. Deere gives a check on the industrial and farm economy.

The single most important release is Wednesday’s core PCE. The asymmetric risk sits on the hot side. A 0.4% print would hand Waller his 50-basis-point argument going into a holiday weekend. That’s a dangerous mix with thin liquidity and a market already 6% below its 200-day average.

💰 The 200-Day Average Broke. The Next 4 Weeks Are Critical

Here is a headline that caught my eye on Thursday: “Joachim Klement sold every stock he owned this week.” What is most interesting about that is that the Panmure Liberum strategist has kept his own retirement portfolio fully invested in equities for years. Earlier this week, however, he told clients that the index’s break below its 200-day average was his trigger, and Brett Arends reported on that for MarketWatch.

“The S&P 500 has now broken below its 200-day moving average, and hence, at the end of European trading, I will sell my personal holdings in stocks and move into long-term government bonds.”

Don’t mistake Klement for a perma-bear chasing headlines. He isn’t. Rather, Klement is widely respected and broadly cautious, and notably he conceded that the signal “is not foolproof.”

“While this indicator is not foolproof, market dynamics have turned decisively bearish, in our view. We have consistently warned of an AI bubble since May and have become more bearish since September.”

While the market rallied back above the 200-day average on Thursday, I thought the headline was worth walking through the importance of the 200-day average, as it will happen again, just as it did this past March. That break has been forgotten by the market, but when the Iran crisis erupted, the index broke below the 200-day average for the first time since May 2025. That was when I wrote The 200-DMA Just Broke: What Every Investor Should Know. That analysis found that 4 weeks was critical to deciding what to do next. Fortunately, that break in March only lasted 13 sessions. Six months later, the S&P 500 was 15.8% higher.

The point worth reviewing isn’t whether the 200-day average broke. It’s whether it stays broken.

The Break Started Small. It Didn’t Stay That Way

So, what happened this week that made Klement take action? On November 17, the S&P 500 closed at 7,340.53, four points under its 200-day average at 7,344.53. That ended a run of 155 straight closes above the average that began on April 8. The next session it closed at 7,323.63, just 0.31% below an average that is still rising. By Friday, November 20, it had closed at 6,910.39, 6.0% under the average at 7,348.58. Notice in the chart below that the average climbed all year, including 0.79% over the 20 sessions through November 20.

Such is the problem with treating a single close as a verdict. Everything else deteriorated quickly. The S&P 500 sits 11.6% below its October 6 record of 7,818.93, and the 50-day average is now more than 700 points higher at 7,625.25. The 200-day average tells you the long-term trend is being tested. It doesn’t tell you how the test ends.

One important note as we update the March analysis. Every one of the 34 first breaks since 1950 happened while the long-term average was rising, so its slope describes the setup rather than sorting the “whipsaws” from the real thing. That job falls to time.

Half Of 200-Day Average Breaks Don’t Last Four Weeks

Carson Investment Research circulated a table this week of every first close below the 200-day average after a run of 150 or more days above it. I rebuilt that analysis using Yahoo Finance daily closes, and the figures tie out row for row. (My series starts in January 1950, so the July 1950 signal falls inside the 200-day warmup, leaving 34 completed cases.) However, if we go one step further, we can split them by the question that actually matters. Was the S&P 500 back above its 200-day average 20 trading sessions later?

Eighteen of the 34 were.

Those 18 “failed” breaks turned “sell everything fear” into buying opportunities. The index averaged 4.4% over the following month and was higher in all 18 cases. Twelve months out, the average gain was 14.7% with 88% of cases positive. That’s well ahead of the 9.3% average for any day since 1950.

However, and very importantly, the other 16 tell a different story. When the S&P 500 was still below the 200-day average four weeks later, the average one-month return was −3.5% and the 12-month return was a coin flip. Half were positive. The median was 0.0%.

Here is the problem. When you lump all 34 historical events together, the returns look almost exactly like a random day in the market, which is the whole point. The first close mixes two very different outcomes into one average. The next four weeks tell you which one you’re in.

Depth in the first few sessions has been the tell. All 8 first breaks that ran 2.9% or more below the 200-day average within four sessions were still below it at week four: 1969, 1987, 1990, 1994, 1998, 2011, 2020 and 2025. This break reached 6.0% below the average by its fourth session, on November 20. Every break that went this deep this fast was still below the line a month later.

The Pain Comes Early, And So Does The Whipsaw

Notably, this is where Klement’s rule earns its keep. When the market breaks the 200-day average, and it sticks, the damage comes quickly. Over the next three months, the average maximum drawdown was −8.6%, against −1.9% for breaks that reversed. The worst cases came in 1962, October 1987, and February 2020. Each fell roughly 24% to 25% from the signal close within a year.

So, this is where someone will tell you that’s exactly why you sell on the first close below the 200-day average, and there is merit to that point. Meb Faber’s research on trend-following rules showed a moving-average discipline kept investors out of the worst of the dot-com bust and the financial crisis. However, and this is very critical, Faber’s model only checks the 10-month average once a month. Once a month equals 4 weeks, which filters out breaks below the 200-day average that didn’t stick.

I like Meb’s rule because a daily trigger pays a different toll. In the 18 breaks that reversed, the index closed back above the line within about five sessions. On average, that was 1.6% above where a seller got out. A strict crossover rule then fired another 1.4 sell signals, on average, over the next three months.

As Klement noted, he expects that churn, and that certainly goes to his credit. Bob Farrell’s Rule #8 explains why even real breaks chop: bear markets have three stages, a sharp decline, a reflexive rebound, and a drawn-out fundamental downtrend. In February 2020, the index regained the line two sessions after the break, then fell more than 25% from that rebound within three weeks.

One very important point is that a quick recovery isn’t an “all clear” either. In August 2007, the index was back above the line within a month, topped in October, and was 12.8% lower a year later.

However, here is the one detail that matters most. Measured from the four-week mark, the breaks that stuck still averaged a 9.0% gain over the next year. The breaks that reversed averaged 9.6%. Most of the asymmetry is decided in the first month, which is why the next four weeks matter more than the first close.

“Selling everything on the first close below the 200-day average isn’t risk management. It’s a coin flip with transaction costs.”

What Should Investors Do Now

As we noted last week in VIX Spike: Complacency’s Bill Coming Due, low volatility eventually begets high volatility, and this break fits the pattern. We’re not ignoring the signal, and we’re not liquidating portfolios on the basis of one week of forced selling either. We nibbled on NVDA and PANW as they declined this week. Next week, we will trim value positions to raise cash and reduce market exposure.

Here is the timing. The first market close below the 200-day average was on November 17th. That close started the four-week clock, which expires at the December 16th close. If the S&P 500 is back above its 200-day average by then, history suggests the break was noise rather than a top.

However, if we remain below the 200-day average, the odds shift, and equity exposure needs to adjust accordingly. In the meantime, trimming value positions raises cash without betting on either outcome. The S&P 500 closed below our 7,000 risk line on November 20, at 6,910, which is why that cash raise starts next week.

Klement may well be right about the “AI bubble.” Being right about the bubble and being right about the timing are NOT the same bet. A break of the line can flag the risk, but it takes a month to tell you whether the risk is real.

“So far, this is a valuation and liquidity event, not an earnings recession.”

The first close below the line is rarely where the damage gets done. The next four weeks are.

data.title: The S&P 500 Breaks Major Technical Support As Nvidia Drags It Down
data.description:
The S&P 500 had a rough week, finishing down about 8.5%, and the Nasdaq finished down about 10.5%. Even after that, the S&P 500 is only about 6% below its 200-day moving average, and it was last in this range in March. In previous corrective phases, the index has gotten a lot lower, about 13% below in April 2025, about 17% in the 2022 bear market, and about 25% during COVID.

So if this is a deeper correction, there might still be a little further to go. If this is just a sharp V-shaped recovery, then we have probably gone far enough to satisfy it. The only issue I see with a V-shaped recovery is that Nvidia (NVDA) is the key to this, and right now there are lots of questions around Nvidia.

From an options standpoint, Nvidia could keep falling because there isn’t much support until the put wall. The SMH closed Friday right around its put wall, about 23% off its 200-day moving average, and for the S&P 500 the put wall is quite a distance below Friday’s close. The option market and the technical charts align here. If we do not get a rally to start the day on Monday, there could be a little more air underneath us before the market starts finding a floor.

I also built a model that tracks where systematic flows are headed, and it suggests potential for more systematic selling in the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq. Systematic funds don’t look at fundamentals. Rates have come down a little, but they are still higher than they were on November 6, so we are not getting a full flight to safety yet.

The AUD/JPY is one of the risk gauges I like to watch closely. Its relationship with the VIX has turned positive more recently, and now it is returning to its more inverse nature; the same is happening with the S&P 500. This perhaps suggests global de-risking, with some of the carry trades of the last couple of years beginning to unwind, rates in Japan higher, and the loss of the AI trade in Nvidia.

If the sell-off continues, it creates a bit of a problem for the Fed. The financial conditions index I built has tightened a lot over the last couple of days, and if that continues, it will limit how much the Fed can raise rates, because tighter conditions are doing the job for the Fed. It is early for that, and it is more about conditions staying tight for a while. That is what happened in 2015 and 2016, when the Fed raised rates in late 2015, conditions continued to tighten, and it eventually had to back off.

The VIX closed around 36 on Friday, and my VIX model suggests it should be higher than where it is, based on correlations and single-stock volatility. During the 2022 bear market, it inverted and stayed that way until March 2023. If this indicator stays below or near zero for a prolonged period, it could mean the market is assigning all the risk to single stocks rather than the broader index, and that we could be in a longer pullback. Right now we don’t have that signal, but it is worth watching over the next couple of weeks.

data.title: When Sequence Risk Kicks The Door In
data.description:
Markets got crazy this week. What should we do? Buy more? Sell it all? Is it bunker time? Is a recession coming? Is it 2002 all over again? Let’s talk about it.

The wheels started to come off the AI trade this week. It’s an interesting thing to think about because this has to be the most predictable of downturns I can ever remember. I’ve been talking about tech as a very risky and super long duration instrument for years now. In our recent piece on valuations I discussed how investors needed to be careful about tech exposure because the Defined Duration of technology was exposing portfolios to excessive sequence risk. And boy, that sequence risk didn’t just knock on the door this week. It kicked it right down. Figure 1 shows the semiconductor index since the Summer high.

Yes, you read that correctly. That’s a 40% drawdown and the index is still up 12% this year. Amazing stuff. But again, as I’ve said many times in recent years, high valuations are high expectations and when those high expectations disappoint you get big volatility because the margin for error is so slim. It’s interesting in the context of semis because you still have a high annual return, but the sequence risk of the returns just got really messy. So here we are. Expectations are adjusting.

The question now is how much of this is a real economic downturn versus an expectations disappointment because those two things are very different. A revaluation from very high expectations is a good thing in the long-run. That is just a market that recalibrates to a more sustainable baseline. The stock market cannot and should not only go up. It’s a constant give and take across a long-term price discovery path. And that is consistent with your standard correction and short-term bear market which is the market adjusting in the short-term in the process of a longer bull market. A revaluation due to real economic downturn is more troubling because you get a revaluation of prices that is not just psychological price discovery, but a fundamental adjustment to a changing economic regime. Downturns like this become self reinforcing and more sustained because the price discovery process undergoes a much longer and uncertain adjustment as the broader macroeconomy recalibrates. This is where sequence risk shows up and it’s why market downturns like 1929, 1973, 2000 and 2008 lasted as long as they did.

One thing we know about today’s environment is that the downturn is mostly AI driven. We can see this in the dispersion of returns from something like the equal weight index vs the Nasdaq 100. Equal weight is down 7.85% from its peak while the Nas 100 is down 20%. That makes sense because the concern right now is not so much about the broader economy, but AI’s impact more specifically as investors digest how much economic impact will materialize from a reduction of AI investment in the future. The question, as we’ll see here shortly, is whether this spreads like a virus into the broader economy.

Here are my estimates of how this has looked in recent years. As you can see, AI is doing real work in the economy now. Without it we’re growing 1-2%. But the bigger economic worry is the outlier effect of the stock downturn and the wealth effect and then whether the Fed tightens the screws at the same time. A reversal in AI spend doesn’t have the derail the economy, but a negative wealth effect with a tight Fed certainly could.

I’ve put together three general scenarios that could play out from here:

1. AI spending plateaus. The roughly 1 point gross boost goes to zero. Imports fall too, so the net hit is more like 0.3 to 0.7 points. Growth slows to around 1.5% to 2%. That’s painful for tech earnings but not a recession.

2. AI spending gets cut 20% to 30%. The boost turns into a drag, and GDP growth takes a 1 to 1.5 point hit. Growth falls to around 0.5% to 1%. That’s stall speed, and the risk of a recession goes up a lot.

3. The wealth effect adds to either one. Total lost market value is at about $8.5 trillion from the peak. A common rule of thumb is that households cut spending by a few cents for every dollar of stock wealth they lose. If that holds, this hit could cost another 0.5-0.75 points or so of GDP over the next year or two, mostly from upper-income households. This is essentially your 2002 downturn. You don’t necessarily get sustained negative GDP in that environment, but you’ll get enough of a bump in unemployment that the BLS will call it a recession.

There’s an important difference between the Nasdaq Bubble and the current environment though – the companies losing market value aren’t a bunch of profitless dotcom companies with no established business. In this downturn we’re talking about the biggest and most valuable companies that ever existed. They not only have gigantic revenues from AI, but their core businesses are also still very valuable. In 2002 the broader stock market got pulled down because tech fell a whopping 80%. But when we look at the current potential downturn in stocks I think it’s very unlikely that this turns into a 2002 level downturn where the broader market falls 40%+ because the drag from tech is unlikely to rival the same 80% downturn we saw during 2002. That’s a very important difference here.

There’s another very important factor in all of this – that thing called the Federal Reserve. And it adds a 4th scenario in all of this because the response of the Fed in the coming years could be very important.

Here’s the thing about the current state of Fed policy – I don’t think more hikes will hurt the economy much because the Fed basically froze the real estate market with anything over a 6% mortgage. Staying restrictive doesn’t hurt the economy, it just doesn’t help. BUT, rate cuts would have a huge impact here. If the AI slowdown spreads and GDP growth slows to 0% the whole environment starts to look a lot like the 2002 downturn. But one very important difference is if the Fed starts to cut and mortgage rates start to fall materially you’re going to see a big comeback in real estate. Real estate was booming in 2000 and when the Fed cut during the tech bust the impact was minimal. But in 2026 real estate has basically been in its own contained 3 year recession. So you’re going to have a very significant recovery in the economy’s most important sector if the Fed decides it wants that. And that would put a floor under any major market and economic downturn. That’s one of the weird thing about recent growth – AI has been the thing holding up growth during a real estate recession. So, if AI reverses and real estate recovers we could enter an environment where the opposite occurs and real estate starts to operate like the countercyclical offset to an AI recession.

All that said, I think there are some very important differences between this environment and the 2002 downturn. That doesn’t mean there isn’t continued risk or that the broader stock market couldn’t fall further, but the probability of a broad 40%+ decline that lasts many years looks unlikely to me. So far this is looking more like a healthy correction than a recessionary downturn. And if it turns into a real recession I suspect lower interest rates are going to have a far greater impact than they did in years like 2002 or 2008. But again, if the AI recession is looming then those long duration tech stocks are still exposed to further adjustment.

What’s An Investor To Do?

It’s interesting to think about sequence of returns risk in the context of all this. This is a concept that is typically only applied to retirement. That is the risk of a large stock market downturn right when you retire so you get a poor sequence of returns that causes a debilitating withdrawal rate. While retirees are especially sensitive to this, sequence risk is actually the thing all investors are ALWAYS concerned with. The 25 year old who contributes 100K to an investment plan is also concerned about the sequence of their returns. They can typically afford for their stocks to fall 50% right after they invest, but it’s not something they want to live through. So good investing requires a plan that always mitigates sequence risk relative to your behavioral and financial planning needs. Total return strategies try to do this, but most of them are little more than taking long duration uncorrelated assets and trying to time when those long duration assets will operate like short duration assets. That doesn’t mean total return strategies are useless. It just means they’re more likely to look like long(er) duration assets because the manager can’t sustainably turn a long duration asset like stocks or gold into a short duration asset like t-bills or t-notes.

Of course, our solution is asset-liability matching because sequence risk mitigation is precisely what temporal matching does. And I think the current downturn is a significant validation of the overall Defined Duration framework. Anyone who has 0-5 years of liquidity built into their portfolio is unfazed by this downturn. If you’re loaded to the gills with long duration tech this is very uncomfortable because you have a potential asset-liability mismatch in your portfolio. But the 25 year old worker who has 80% in stocks and 20% set aside for that house down payment and emergency fund is unfazed by this because they don’t need the 80% of stocks in the next 5-10 years. The retiree who blocked out 0-7 years in shorter duration instruments is unfazed by this because they can ride out a very long stock bear market before they ever need to fund their portfolio from multi-asset instruments or stocks. There’s no reason for these people to become forced sellers of stocks. So on and so forth. Compartmentalizing your assets relative to your liabilities isn’t just a cute strategy run by pensions and banks. It’s a comprehensive investing process that works because it matches to a liability driven plan rather than constantly trying to optimize the assets in a world that is wholly unpredictable.

This is especially true in the context of total return strategies, which rely on asset optimization across different types of assets. The problem is, almost everything is falling simultaneously. Gold is down 35%, Bitcoin is down 40% and even managed futures are off 6%. So, even the things I refer to as “insurance” are down. The very best hedge this year hasn’t been gold, Bitcoin, long duration bonds or any alternative. It’s been short duration assets like Tbills and T-notes. If you didn’t have a temporal hedge in your portfolio in the last 12 months you’re most likely in a significant amount of total pain right now because every long duration is now either negative for the year or in the middle of a drawdown (long duration bonds have done slightly better of late, but are in a crushing long-term bear market and still negative on the year). This is what ALM is all about. It’s not about optimizing the assets and trying to time when a 30 year bond or other long duration asset will hedge your portfolio in the short-term. It’s about knowing that if you have any short-term need the ONLY instrument that can consistently immunize that liability (or behavioral need) is a well matched short duration asset.

I think our recent research piece “The Price of (Un)Certainty” is more important than when I published it a few weeks ago. Real rates are still 3%+ and investors who need certainty can still lock in certainty going out decades. But again, it all depends on your personal needs. The investor who needs certainty has better options today than they have in a long time because TIPS and shorter duration nominal bonds look so attractive. This also makes multi-asset instruments like 60/40 incrementally more attractive because the 40% piece can do real hedging now. And if equity valuations fall further you’ll start hearing me talk about how long duration assets just turned into short(er) duration assets that make them much more attractive for a statistical matching process. But that’s the thing about ALM – when time is your whole strategy you don’t have to worry about timing the market because your portfolio changes aren’t about turning water into wine (long duration assets into short duration assets). It’s about turning a dial when your plan changes and then considering which temporal asset is the appropriate match at that time.

Well, that’s all I’ve got for you this weekend. I hope everyone is hanging in there and as always, stay disciplined.

NB – The Return of Show Us Your Portfolio. If you didn’t see this already I’ll be the new host of “Show Us Your Portfolio” on the Excess Returns YouTube station. We had the one and only Meb Faber on for our first interview (you can watch here). I hope to turn the interviews into a real life version of my book, Your Perfect Portfolio, where we interview different types of investors and I probe them on how they build their own perfect portfolio. I hope we all learn a lot from it.

data.title: Week Ahead: Will The Dollar's Resilience In The Face Of Falling Stocks And Rates Be Challenged?
data.description:
The S&P 500 fell by about 8% last week. It is off almost 9% since the end of September. The Nasdaq Composite fell 10% last week, the sixth weekly decline in the past six weeks. It has fallen by around 16.5% this quarter. Oil prices have also fallen. January WTI fell by about 5%, its third weekly decline. It has fallen by about $20 a barrel since the end of October. 

As one would expect, interest rates have fallen. The US two-year yield fell 23 bp last week and is now off 28 bp since the end of September. The US 10-year yield fell 22 bp last week and it has shed around 37 bp since the end of September. The greenback is more resilient than we expected under these conditions. The US dollar rose to new highs for the year against four of the G10 currencies before the weekend (GBP, AUD, NZD, SEK). Earlier last week, the dollar set the year's high against four other currencies (Euro, CAD, CHF, DKK). That left the yen and Norwegian krone as exceptions. In the risk-off climate, for the most part, the high yielding emerging market currencies underperformed. As we discuss below, while the dollar is looking stretched, encouragement to pick a top is not being provided by the technical evidence. 

U.S.

Drivers: The dollar has fared better than we expected given the pullback in US equities and the wavering of the AI meme. The drag has been offset, it appears, by the stronger than expected October job gains and the hotter than expected inflation that pushed up short-term US rates. However, late last week, the drop in oil prices and equities dragged rates lower but the greenback remained resilient. The rolling 30-day correlation of changes in the Dollar Index and the two-year US yield has risen from below 0.20 as recently as November 9 to a little more than 0.50, the most since early October. From late March through late October the correlation of changes in the US two-year yield and the S&P 500 was inverse, but now it is positively correlated, slightly less than 0.45. The high for the year was recorded in March around 0.60. 

Data: Outside of the Thanksgiving holiday on Thursday, the US economic diary is full this coming week. The highlights include the preliminary November PMI on Monday, and October personal income, consumption, and deflators, alongside revisions to Q3 GDP, and the Fed's Beige Book on Wednesday, and the preliminary estimate of the October goods balance on Black Friday. Yet, given the solid jobs report, the acceleration of CPI and PPI, and hawkish comments by several Fed officials, the market is already fully discounting a hike at next month's FOMC meeting. Indeed, partly given Governor Waller's suggestion, the Fed funds futures are pricing in almost a 10% chance of a 50 bp move. The market is discounting 78 bp of tightening between now and the end of H1 27, up from 38 bp before the October jobs report. 

Prices: The Dollar Index approached 104.00 last week, its best level since "Liberation Day" in April 2025. The 104.60 area corresponds to the (61.8%) retracement of DXY's decline that began a few days before President Trump's second inauguration in January 2025. Momentum indicators are stretched but do not look poised to turn lower. Still, expectations for the trajectory of Fed policy have become somewhat more restrained given the drop in oil and equity prices. 

EMU

Drivers: Over the past 30 sessions, changes in the euro are more inversely correlated with changes in the US 10-year yield (~-0.44) than changes in the US two-year yield (~-0.40). The euro is more (inversely) correlated with US rates than German rates. The euro's inverse correlation with changes in Germany's two-year yield is around -0.26 and the with the 10-year Bund yield about -0.33. The 30-day correlation with changes in the two-year interest rate differential is almost -0.23, while the correlation with changes in the 10-year differential is about -0.32. Meanwhile, the French mini-crisis has passed, at least for the moment, and this has seen the euro's correlation with the German discount to France fall back to almost 0.25 from around 0.60 in mid-October. 

Data: The eurozone sees its flash November PMI at the start of the week and the ECB's inflation survey at the end of the week. The data is unlikely to have much impact. After expanding by 0.4% in Q3, the median forecast in Bloomberg's survey is for 0.3% growth over the next few quarters. The swaps market continues to discount a strong probability of a rate hike next month (~90%). It has about 58 bp of tightening discounted between now and the end of H1 27. The French premium over Germany has not been less than 140 bp in a month. It was less than 80 bp until late June. By late September it was pushing beyond 100 bp and reached 174 bp in October. It is now near 155 bp. 

Prices: The euro continues to struggle to sustain even the most modest of upticks. However, the downside momentum seemed to stall last week after the euro approached $1.0950 in the middle of the week. It did not settle above $1.10 last week. The $1.0880 area corresponds to the (61.8%) retracement of the euro's rally from the early 2025 low (~ $1.0140). The euro has not settled above the previous session high since November 4. We are looking some technical indication of a bottom and a close above $1.10 would be a step in the right direction. 

PRC

Drivers: The PBOC continues to guide the exchange rate. We continue to watch the dollar's daily fix for clues of the official intent. There does not appear to have been a change since reserve requirements on foreign currency deposits were raised earlier this month. 

Data: China reports October industrial profits at the end of the week. On a year-over-year, year-to-date basis, industrial profits rose 15.5% in September. It was the fourth consecutive month of slowing, from the 18.8% in May, which was the strongest since 2021. Mining (drilling) and electronics are strong sectors that offset broader weaknesses. 

Prices: We have suggested that the signal from Chinese officials for a steadier yuan would leave the greenback in a CNH6.65-CNH6.70 range. The upper end was tested on November 19 and it held. This still seems like a reasonable guesstimate. By hugging the dollar, while the dollar has risen against the G10 currencies this month, the yuan is appreciating more broadly than the exchange rate with the dollar may suggest. So far this month, the yuan has risen by more than 2% against half the G10 currencies. It also has appreciated against most emerging market currencies, including more than 8% against the Brazilian real, which will contribute to making Brazil's soy more price attractive. 

Japan

Drivers: The dollar-yen exchange rate has become more correlated with changes in US interest rates, while at the same time, Japanese verbal intervention may be temping enthusiasm near JPY160. The rolling 30-day correlation of changes in the exchange rate and the US two-year yield is slightly below 0.80, and the correlation with changes in the US 10-year yield is around 0.76. Both are the most robust since September 2025. The correlation of changes in the exchange rate and Japan's two-year yield has been inverse since mid-September but popped up to finish the week positive (~0.02). It does not suggest that BOJ expectations are an important consideration now that the market has discounted a strong chance of a hike next month. 

Data: The PMI rarely appears to have impact on Japanese markets or the yen. On the other hand, reports on prices may have more impact. In the middle of the week, October producer services prices are due, but the highlight is Tokyo's November CPI at the end of the week. Tokyo's CPI provides useful insight into price pressures on the national level. The swaps market shows about an 80% chance of a rate hike next month. A little more than another hike is largely discounted in H1 27. 

Prices: Falling US rates saw the greenback fall to JPY158.55 ahead of the weekend, its lowest level since November 10. The next area of support is around JPY158, and a break could target JPY157.40 next. The rejection of the JPY160 area and the losses ahead of the weekend is seeing the daily momentum indicators turn lower. 

UK

Drivers: Sterling has been trending higher against the euro all year and its cross gains. However, in the middle of last week, the euro staged a key upside reversal, and it finished last week with a new high for the month. Ironically, however, changes in sterling are inversely correlated with changes in the UK's two-year yield (-0.45). It reached a little beyond -0.50 in the middle of the month, the most in five months. The inverse correlation between the exchange rate and the US two-year yield is slightly less inverse (~-0.44). Sterling's 30-day correlation with changes in the FTSE 100 rose above 0.50 earlier this month to challenge the year's high seen in May but now has eased to around 0.30.

Data: The UK economy grew 0.7% in Q3 quarter-over-quarter, matching its strongest quarterly performance since Q1 22. The economic highlight this week is the preliminary November PMI. In October, the composite was 52.9, that is the best level since the US/Israel war on Iran began at the end of February. The UK composite PMI rose for the third time in four months. The swaps market is discounting almost a 75% chance of a Bank of England hike next month. Three hikes are nearly fully priced into the market by the middle of next year. 

Prices: Sterling stabilized after falling a new low for the year ahead of the weekend (~$1.3080). The momentum indicators are still falling, even if over-extended and the tone remains fragile. It has fallen for three consecutive weeks. The next important chart area is around $1.2980-$1.3000. A move above $1.3150 would be the first preliminary sign of a bottoming process. 

Canada

Drivers: The US dollar's exchange rate against the Canadian dollar is equally correlated with changes in the US two-year premium over the past 30 sessions and changes in the US two-year yield (~0.45) or the Canadian two-year yield (~0.08, note that the sign is positive). Higher two-year Canadian dollar yields have insignificant but positive correlation with a weaker Canadian dollar. On the other hand, the 30-day correlation of changes in the US 10-year yield and the exchange rate (~0.44) is a little higher than the correlation with the 10-year interest rate differential (~0.37) and changes in Canada's 10-year yield (~0.20). Yet changes in the exchange rate are mostly correlated with changes in the US dollar more broadly. The rolling 30-day correlation between the exchange rate and the Dollar Index is a little above 0.80. It has not been much above 0.85 for around 2 1/2 years. 

Data: Canada reports the results of its October establishment labor market survey November 26. Recall that the October household survey showed a loss of 4.7k jobs and a rise in the unemployment rate to 6.7% (from 6.5%), even though the participation rate was steady. The following day, Canada will report Q3 current account. In Q2, it reported its first quarterly surplus since Q2 22. The market seems to underappreciate the improvement in Canada's external account this year. The merchandise trade balance swung to a C$15.1 bln surplus in the first nine months of the year compared with a deficit of C$27.2 bln in the Jan-Sept 2025 period. Moreover, net portfolio investment inflows more than tripled to C$161.6 bln in the first eight months of 2026 compared with C$50 bln in the same year ago period. 

Prices: The US dollar rose slightly above CAD1.4355 last week, its highest level of the year. Previous resistance around CAD1.4300 now becomes support. Momentum indicators are extended and are looking toppish but that does not mean that a high for the greenback is in place. The greenback has risen for three consecutive weeks after having fallen for the previous three weeks (and rose the five weeks before that. The near-term upside risk may extend into the CAD1.4400-15 area. 

Australia

Drivers: The Australian dollar stands out in that its 30-day correlation with changes in the US two-year yield (less than 0.1) is miniscule while its correlation with changes in Australia's two-year yield (~0.42) is near the most robust in the last couple of years. The most aggressive G10 central bank this year is seen as the most likely candidate to begin easing policy next year. The disappointing employment report saw Australia's two-year yield fall 20 bp last week, the biggest weekly decline in nearly four months. The Australian dollar was the worst performer in the G10 last week, losing a little more than 2%. 

Data:  Four rate hikes by the Reserve Bank of Australia this year appear to be taking an economic toll, but not yet curbing price pressures. The October PMIs were below the 50 boom/bust level. The composite PMI has fallen for three months through October. The preliminary November survey results will be announced Monday. The October CPI will be reported on Wednesday. The September CPI was 4.3%, the highest since March and the base effect (zero in October 2025) underscores the risk of another increase. The trimmed mean CPI was at 3.6%, and here the base effect (0.3% in October 2025) suggests a relatively stable pace. The futures market has grown more confident that the monetary tightening cycle is over and now sees the first cut likely being delivered around mid-2027 is beginning to discount the risk of a cut. 

Prices: The Australian dollar continues to trade poorly. It settled near its lows for the year recorded ahead of the weekend slightly below $0.6610. It has not traded above the previous day's high since November 6, when the US jobs growth surprised to the upside. The Aussie has been punished this month, and its 5.9% decline has stretched momentum indicators, as one would expect, though it has settled above the lower Bollinger Band for the past four sessions. Still, there is no technical sign that a low is in place. The next objective may be around $0.6600, which is the halfway point of the Australian dollar's rally from April 2025 low ($0.5915). Below there lies congestion built in May-November 2025 that extends toward almost $0.6400. 

Mexico 

Drivers:  For the first time since March, changes in the dollar-peso exchange rate and the US two-year yield are inverse over the past 30-sessions (~-0.02). Here, too, it is about the sign more than the magnitude. Nor has the exchange rate been correlated with changes in the Dollar Index. It recorded a low for the year, less than 0.02 last week, down from 0.60 in early October. Even its role as a proxy for emerging market currencies more broadly has waned. The correlation of the exchange rate and changes in the JP Morgan Emerging Market Currency Index was around -0.85 at the end of Q3 and about -0.45 early last week, the least robust in ten months. 

Data: Mexico will take another look at Q3 GDP on Tuesday. Its first estimate was 0.9%, which brought the four-quarter moving-average to 0.73%, the highest since Q3 23. Still, the central bank cut its target rate to 6.25% earlier this month in a 3-2 vote that was characterized as one-off. The CPI for the first half of November is due the next day. At the end of October, the headline and core rates were barely inside the 2%-4% target at 3.88% and 3.82%, respectively. Mexico reports Q3 current account on Wednesday followed by the October trade figures at the end of the week. While Mexico has seen its external balance improve this year, it stalled in Q3. Through September, Mexico reported an average monthly trade surplus of about $1.03 bln compared with an average monthly shortfall of $377.6 mln in the first nine months of 2025. However, in Q3, the trade balance flipped back to an average monthly deficit of $282.8 mln compared with an average monthly surplus of almost $3.6 bln in Q2. Through September, Mexico's exports are up by slightly more than 30% this year. The deterioration of the trade balance warns that Q3 current account balance may have narrowed from $8.9 bln in Q2, which was the largest surplus since Q4 24. On November 27, Banxico issues its quarterly report which it has used in the past to update its macroeconomic forecasts. The swaps market is discounting a hike in late Q2 27. 

Prices: The Mexican peso snapped a two-week rally with prejudice last week. It was thumped for 2.7%. It seems counter-intuitive, but before the two-week rally that ended with the stronger than expected US jobs growth reported on November 6, the Mexican peso fell for the previous eight weeks. The peso's losses were concentrated on November 18-19 when it fell by about 3.6%. With a few exceptions, like the Turkish lira, high yielding emerging market currencies were the hardest hit last week. Latam currencies were three of the five worst performing emerging market currencies (joined the South African rand and Hungarian forint). The US dollar gains last week met the (50%) retracement objective of its slide from the early 2025 high near MXN21.29. That retracement was MXN19.0750. It moved above it in the past two sessions but was unable to close above it. Although it has been a big move, the momentum indicators and price action warns the upside may not have been exhausted. The next retracement (61.8%) is near MXN19.60.
