Today we continue my series on debt and taxes. In brief, the federal government has a huge amount of spending, a less huge amount of tax revenue, and thus a huge debt. Almost everyone agrees we need to close this gap. We differ on how to do so.

Last week we looked at just income taxes. This week we are going to look at other types of US taxes as necessary groundwork for when we look at what the outcome of raising various taxes will be, either with or without accompanying spending cuts. Then we will start on how effective simply raising taxes will be. I expect that to be at least one if not two more letters.

There are two knobs we can turn: more/less spending and more/less taxes. We can turn one of them, both of them or neither of them. Specifically, can we make a dent in the debt by raising taxes on the wealthiest taxpayers? That’s politically appealing to some because it leaves most voters unaffected, though it may affect the economy by reducing growth as it has elsewhere. That being said, there is serious research that shows taxes can raised somewhat without too much drag on the economy, but nowhere near enough to solve the problem.

The problem with simply taxing the rich more, as you’ll see, is that it won’t solve the problem, because it changes behavior and thus eventual taxes. The debt will still be there and the voters we are trying to shield will still get hurt.

A Quick Look at Social Security

I will go deeper on Social Security in a future letter. It deserves more than a short mention. But since payroll taxes are a giant part of all federal revenue – and Social Security benefits comprise a giant part of federal spending – I want to run through a few preliminary numbers now.

Social Security at a Glance

Sources: SSA (wage base); 2026 Social Security Trustees Report as summarized by CRS and others; Mauldin Economics, John Mauldin

Because of the wage cap, the payroll tax is a flat tax up to $184,500 and zero above it. That makes it regressive at the top, which is exactly why "raise the cap" is always on the list of fixes. We will run those numbers when we get there.

Up to 85% of benefits can be subject to income tax for retirees above certain income thresholds. The tax on the first half of benefits goes back into the Social Security trust funds, about $58 billion in 2025; the tax on the portion between 50% and 85% goes to Medicare's hospital insurance fund. The income thresholds have not been adjusted for inflation since 1993, so every year more retirees get caught. This has quietly been propping up the trust funds. (See, sometimes inflation helps! – note sarcasm) The new senior deduction in last year's tax bill further reduced Social Security revenue, though temporarily as the $6,000 tax break expires in 2028.

Overall, the system’s costs have exceeded its tax revenue since 2010 and exceeded total income, including interest, since 2021. The trust fund is not a vault. It is an IOU from the Treasury, and the Treasury has to borrow to redeem it. As I said, this will take a full letter, because they’re just 100 nuances. There are almost 60 million Americans receiving Social Security.

The total Social Security beneficiary population (all ages) is over 76 million people in October 2026, but the vast majority are older adults. Most paid Social Security taxes for their entire adult lives and have the entirely reasonable expectation that they will get those benefits when they retire.

According to the U.S. Census Bureau’s analysis of survey responses matched with IRS tax and Social Security Administration benefit records, about 14%, or 22 million, older Americans receive 90% or more of their household income from Social Security. Survey data, which is subject to the vagaries of survey questions, suggest that the number might be as much as twice that. There are reasons for this discrepancy, and we will walk into that minefield in a later letter.

Corporate Tax Rates

The corporate income tax is a much smaller part of the picture than its political profile suggests, amounting to only about 7% of federal revenue last year. The 2017 tax law cut the rate from 35% to 21%. Here is what happened to receipts.

Corporate income tax receipts and the statutory rate.

Receipts fell sharply in the first three years after the cut, as everyone expected. Then they climbed to records: $425 billion in fiscal 2022 and $530 billion in fiscal 2024, far more than the government ever collected at 35%. Supporters of lower rates point to this as evidence that a lower rate can bring in as much or more revenue over time, by keeping profits and headquarters in the US and reducing the incentive to shift income abroad.

There is research behind that view. Kevin Hassett and Alex Brill found a corporate "Laffer curve" across developed countries, with the revenue-maximizing rate drifting down toward about 26%; Kimberly Clausing's basic estimate was about 33%. Both were above the 21% we have now, and both were below the 35% we had before 2017.

On the other hand, the Congressional Research Service disputes those findings and argues that most of the post-2021 surge reflects inflation and unusually high corporate profits rather than the rate cut. And receipts fell to $381 billion in fiscal 2026, in part because last year's tax law restored full expensing for business investment. This requires a little deeper dive.

First, the law that allows businesses to deduct ordinary and necessary business expenses was first established in the Internal Revenue Code of 1954, and has been amended several times since then, most recently and significantly in 2017 in the first Trump administration. Going forward, the details matter if we are going to consider raising corporate tax rates again.

  • Prior to 2025, 100% bonus depreciation had been available under the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) for qualified property placed in service between September 27, 2017, and the end of 2022

  • The TCJA introduced a phase‑out: 80% in 2023, 60% in 2024, 40% in 2025, 20% in 2026, and 0% by 2027

  • The OBBBA restored the 100% rate and made it permanent for qualified property placed in service after January 19, 2025 

  • This applies to most tangible personal property with a recovery period of 20 years or less, certain software, and other qualifying assets, allowing corporations to deduct the full cost in the first year instead of depreciating over time.

The purpose behind accelerated depreciation is to give businesses incentive to invest money sooner than they might otherwise. And it clearly works. And while it costs “tax revenue" to allow for earlier depreciation, over time it evens out. Let's say that a particular widget would normally depreciate over five years. It would be the same total deduction whether it is over one or five years, so over time, the revenues will equal out. But the theory is the economy is growing faster. The counterargument is that businesses will make the investment anyway. In some cases, this is very likely true. But not in all cases.

My own reading is that above some point higher corporate tax rates cost more in lost investment than they bring in, and that the 35% we had before 2017 was well above that point, one of the highest in the developed world. 21% is a great number as it makes us competitive with countries like Ireland that have lower rates. But could we increase it to 25% or some higher number? When we are raising taxes everywhere else because of the deficit and debt? If we are going to solve the debt crisis, everything has to be on the table.

Longtime readers will know that my default position is for lower taxes and smaller government. But in what I believe is the coming sovereign debt crisis, people of good faith on all sides are going to have to make compromises. And as I keep repeating, no one will like them. They will all be bad choices.

Here’s another look at a chart I shared last week. Note how the individual income tax and payroll taxes dwarf corporate income tax revenue.

Below the corporate tax are some even smaller categories: Tariffs, excise taxes (gasoline, etc.), estate and gift taxes, etc. These generate much more heat than they do money for the government. Even Trump’s new tariffs – which have caused real economic damage – are a rounding error in the big picture. They grew a lot in percentage terms, from $79.1 billion in FY 2024 to $194.9 billion in FY 2025. My preference would be to have a low and standard flat tariff if we have any tariff at all, rather than using tariffs as a hammer to bludgeon our trading partners. Are there cases can be made for a tariff? Yes, and they should be on the table.

Then there’s the estate tax. Very few estates actually pay it because very few estates are bigger than the excluded amount. The few that are bigger can usually avoid it by employing (perfectly legal) estate planning techniques. The estate tax is as close as we get to a “voluntary” tax. Anyone who actually pays it does so by default.

Now, About Taxing the Rich

We now have enough data to begin do the arithmetic. Let's first be generous to the idea and assume, unrealistically, that nobody changes their behavior. No one moves, no one realizes fewer capital gains, no one restructures a business or hires a better accountant. These are static numbers, using 2023 income against the 2026 deficit.

"Tax the Rich" vs. the Deficit (static estimates, no behavioral response)

Sources: IRS Statistics of Income via Tax Foundation (tax year 2023); CBO; Forbes; Mauldin Economics static calculations; Mauldin Economics, John Mauldin.

Read that table slowly. First note that the reason the top 1% only pay 26.3% of their income as taxes, is that much of their income is capital gains and other tax-favored income. They will pay the full 39.9% on their non-capital gain or tax-sheltered income. To get them to pay 40% you would have to exclude capital gains taxes above a certain number. Again, that assumes no behavior changes which is not realistic.

Raising the average tax rate on the top 1% by more than half, from 26.3% to 40%, which would require top marginal rates far above today's 39.9% (including the Medicare tax), raises about $430 billion on paper. That closes about a fifth of the gap. To close the whole deficit through the income tax on the rich, you would have to take essentially every dollar the top 1% earns, after what they already pay, and they would have to keep earning it anyway.

Static revenue from taxing the rich vs. the deficit.

Wealth taxes don’t escape the arithmetic either. The Forbes 400 are worth a record $8 trillion this year. Seize all of it, every share of every company, and you could pay for about four years of deficits. Once. Then it would be gone, along with the companies those shares represent being run by people with every incentive to make them grow.

And those are the generous numbers. In the real world, behavior changes. Top incomes are dominated by capital gains, which people can choose when to realize. Top-end income is also volatile: in 2023 the income of the top 1% fell 9%, mostly because of lower realized capital gains. We have been in an extraordinarily powerful bull market which allows for extraordinarily high capital gains. A bear market will eviscerate those potential gains.

Raise the rate sharply and gains get realized less often, held until death, or moved into structures that are taxed later or not at all. The revenue estimates shrink. That is Adam Smith's fourth maxim in action.

Let me be clear about what I am and am not saying. I am not saying the rich cannot or should not pay more. There may be good arguments for some increases at the top, and we will look at them fairly. What I am saying is that "tax the rich" cannot, by itself, come anywhere close to closing a $2 trillion deficit, much less pay for new spending on top of it. The math simply doesn’t work. The people making that promise are either not doing the arithmetic or hoping you will not.

The Scorecard

Pulling the key numbers together in one place:

IRS figures are tax returns, tax year 2023. CBO figures are households, 2023, and include payroll, corporate and excise taxes. n/a: not published on that basis. Sources: IRS SOI; Tax Foundation; CBO; Mauldin Economics, John Mauldin.

The rich pay most of the income tax already. The middle pays mostly payroll taxes (which are quite real, especially in percentage of total income terms). The bottom 40-50% as a group is a net recipient of government subsidies as we demonstrated last week. And the income tax, whatever its top rate, has brought in roughly 7% to 10% of GDP for 75 years.

Next, we have to ask an uncomfortable question. Suppose we tried to get the deficit below nominal GDP growth using taxes alone. How much would we need to raise? From whom? Through what kind of tax? Since 86% of revenue comes from individual income and payroll taxes, any serious income tax-only plan has to reach deep into the middle class, or find another revenue source. For instance, the average OECD country gets 31% of their tax revenues from consumption taxes, either direct sales taxes or the much larger case of value-added taxes (VAT).

In future letters we will look at what various rate increases would actually raise, what the economic research says about the drag on growth, and why most of the developed world funds its welfare states with broad consumption taxes as well as payroll taxes and income taxes rather than by taxing the rich even harder than we already do. (Regular readers will remember I have floated a VAT before, and I want to revisit that idea honestly, warts and all.)

Then we will turn to the other side: what we actually spend money on, line by line, and who depends on each line. Every item in the budget has a constituency. It is one thing to say health care is a large share of federal spending; it is another to tell a specific group of people their benefits will be cut.

Mathematically, you can close the gap with tax increases, spending cuts, or a combination. Politically, you can’t do it with only one of those. That’s why we will likely not do anything substantial until a crisis forces our hand. Stay tuned…

data.title: U.S. Stocks: Look Out Above
data.description:
Week 48 | Outlook: 23–27 November 2026

This week the S&P 500 and Dow joined the Nasdaq in correction territory, with Friday’s brutal selling accelerating into the close, leaving many to ponder which fund(s) had blown up. The S&P (SPX) lost 3.70% on the day and 8.61% on the week, while the Nasdaq Composite (NDX) fell 5.61% on Friday and just over 10% for the week. We think the set up offers scope for a sharp rebound well worth playing for, but the form the bounce takes deserves monitoring closely.

Strong earnings results weren’t enough to change the bearish mood among investors. Nvidia (NVDA) reported quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion and forecast approximately $130 billion for the following quarter, yet its shares continued to freefall. Anthropic’s much anticipated flotation also failed to restore confidence across technology. We believe investors are becoming more demanding about what they’ll pay for future growth, especially where financing, export access and corporate governance complicate the story. A healthy order book doesn’t make the share price inexpensive.

Nor has the retreat produced a uniform rush into defensive assets. Treasuries strengthened, with the ten-year yield reported near 4.91% late on Friday afternoon, while gold remained under pressure. Oil recovered from its earlier Friday losses but still finished another week lower. We think that combination points towards a growing concern about growth and liquidity, rather than a simple inflation trade in which tangible assets rise together. Gold’s failure to benefit from falling bond yields is particularly difficult to ignore.

There is a credible case against assuming the economy is already falling apart. Our macro composite score remains mixed at 54.4 out of 100, and the latest initial unemployment claims release showed 203,000 claims, only a modest increase. Nvidia's results were good. However, with the selling we saw our equity breadth score has weakened to 32.2 and sentiment has fallen to 15.8, classified as extreme fear. We think those readings make a short term rebound in equities more than plausible, and it is likely to be a strong rally.

Most of this week's potential catalysts arrive on Wednesday 25 November, but we wouldn't wait for results to get long. October personal income and outlays, including PCE inflation, arrive alongside the second estimate of third-quarter GDP at 13:30 GMT. Durable goods orders are due at the same time, followed by new home sales at 15:00 and the Fed’s Beige Book at 19:00. HPE’s Monday evening call, followed by Dell (DELL) and Workday (WDAY) on Tuesday evening, gives investors another look at enterprise technology demand. Thanksgiving makes this an unusual five session outlook. US cash equities are closed on Thursday 26 November and finish at 18:00 GMT on Friday 27 November.

US indices: odds favour the bulls this week

The reported positioning change runs from Tuesday 10 November to Tuesday 17 November. Leveraged funds added 52,078 E-mini S&P 500 longs and covered 16,004 shorts, improving their net position by 68,082 contracts. They nevertheless remained net short by 234,978 contracts. That is a substantial reduction in bearish exposure during a falling market, but not a move into an outright net long position. We think that distinction makes this report less reassuring than a casual reading might suggest.

Funds had already used part of their capacity to cover shorts before the subsequent sell-off accelerated. There are still plenty of shorts outstanding, but the report doesn’t show an untouched reservoir of pessimism suddenly waiting to reverse. Our Wednesday–Friday inference is that the renewed selling probably rebuilt some bearish exposure and discouraged the fresh longs added earlier. Monday and Tuesday could still alter that direction before the next positioning observation. Thanksgiving delays publication of that next COT report until Monday 30 November.

The five-year SPY seasonal profile offers a more supportive counterweight. Across 2021–2025, the Week 48 average return was approximately 1.13%, and the seasonal path rises through this part of November. That gives us a reason to take a recovery attempt seriously. Current breadth and sentiment readings support that view. The deterioration has now extended beyond the largest technology shares, and while relatively stronger performance elsewhere can make an equal-weight comparison look encouraging, losing less than the market leader is useful resilience but isn’t the same as broad buying. A decent bounce followed by a retest of the recent lows to give us a breadth washout would be a better marker of a lasting low.

With the sell off emanating from tech, we thought we would take a look at the Nasdaq 100 ETF (QQQ) for a steer on the chances of a recovery. Friday sell offs of 5%+ are quite rare, and in all cases bar the second year of the dot-com bear market we saw sizeable returns over the following week. That is our base case for this week then, but be warned that a lack of upside follow through early on would be an omen of something far more bearish about to play out. For QQQ we have support at 593.86, with resistance at 631.45, 650.90 then 706.64. For SPY we have support at 671.38, with resistance at 723.07 and 740.71.

Gold: much unloved but worth watching

Gold’s Tuesday-to-Tuesday report, covering 10–17 November, shows managed money reducing its net long by 9,399 contracts to 102,942. Long holdings fell by 5,412 contracts while shorts increased by 3,987. The resulting position sits at the 44th percentile of its own 4 year history. Enthusiasm has been reduced, but this is neither a net short market nor an extreme positioning washout. Unfortunately we think there is still room for investors to reduce exposure if the metal continues to disappoint when protection is most wanted.

The Wednesday–Friday inference is for further erosion of that net long. Gold weakened after Tuesday, Thursday’s early recovery failed to establish a durable improvement, and Friday brought renewed pressure even as Treasuries rallied. We think the most likely positioning consequence is continued retreat from bullish exposure. Gold's inability to respond to lower nominal yields suggests that concern about Fed policy is offsetting it's usual defensive appeal.

Seasonality argues against becoming too comfortable with the downside. GLD’s five-year Week 48 average is approximately +1.56%, and its seasonal path improves into late November. We think that raises the chance of a rebound this week in tandem with stocks. Since gold has already failed to deliver the protection that fearful equity sentiment might have suggested, we can assume it now trades in lock-step with equities instead.

Our preferred view is a hesitant start followed by an attempt to stabilise around Wednesday’s inflation release. Softer inflation and a less demanding dollar backdrop would give that recovery a good foundation. We don’t yet expect an immediate return to the earlier uptrend and see a bounce this week as the prelude to further lows ahead. Resistance in GLD is 339.83 with support at 293.70 to 305.63.

Oil: a bounce into a challenging fundamental backdrop

Managed money’s WTI position became more defensive between Tuesday 10 and Tuesday 17 November. Funds added 5,519 longs, but added a much larger 15,419 shorts. The net long consequently fell by 9,900 contracts to just 15,814. Positioning sits at the 7.7th percentile of its own history. This was a change driven by heavier short additions, rather than an across-the-board liquidation of long holdings, and it leaves oil much closer to the pessimistic end of its range than gold.

Our Wednesday–Friday inference is that the week’s renewed weakness probably encouraged further defensive positioning, although Friday’s recovery may have whipsawed the new shorts. Oil’s final session was firmer than the early reports suggested, and gives oil bulls some hope to cling to, but the broader weekly direction remained down. Reports of stronger Middle Eastern exports are weighing against the disruption premium, while Saturday’s fresh report of a tanker strike near Hormuz underlines how quickly the balance can change. We would not treat either additional supply promises or a single incident as proof of an effect on physical deliveries. Definitive supply has become harder to gauge.

The five year USO seasonal pattern is much less friendly than the other three markets. Its Week 48 average return was approximately −0.44%, and the surrounding late-November path is uneven and generally weak. Together with deteriorating risk appetite, that makes us reluctant to interpret the Friday rebound as the start of a new advance. While the net-long positioning is low historically, there is room to drop further and we feel the short term bear case is stronger on balance.

We expect a volatile opening, with weekend shipping headlines capable of extending Friday’s recovery quite sharply. Our preferred path is for that strength to struggle as attention returns to exports, demand and Wednesday’s economic releases, leaving oil vulnerable again into the holiday period. That is a modest bearish preference, not a forecast of an ouright freefall. Resistance in USO stands at 144.90 and 164.67, with support at 138.01 then 124.68.

US bonds: protection comes with crowded positioning

Asset managers increased their net long in US ten-year Treasury futures by 117,073 contracts between Tuesday 10 and Tuesday 17 November, reaching 3,270,834. They added 180,449 longs and 63,376 shorts. The net position stands at the 100th percentile of the recorded historical comparison. This is genuinely a large positive net position, unlike the still-negative S&P stance. We think it provides evidence of substantial institutional commitment to duration, while also warning that an unwinding could result in a sharp decline.

Our Wednesday–Friday inference is that the later Treasury rally probably reinforced that commitment. The strongest defensive response came as equity selling intensified on Friday, and the reported ten-year yield fell to approximately 4.91% late in the afternoon. That is a price observation after the COT cutoff, not evidence that Tuesday’s reported position already captured the rally. We think the next report is more likely to show continued support for duration than a wholesale retreat, unless the first two sessions of the coming week sharply reverse the move.

IEF’s five-year seasonal profile supports the near-term bond case, with a Week 48 average return of approximately +1.39%. Fearful equity sentiment provides another source of demand. The main obstacle is policy: the October Fed minutes, released this week, still described further rate increases as likely appropriate under participants’ baseline outlooks. We believe Wednesday’s inflation figures will further test whether defensive buying can offset that threat.

On balance this week we expect bonds to decline in the face of an equity market bounce that should prompt some profit taking after Friday’s move. A strong inflation release could result in that decline gathering speed. For IEF resistance stands at 92.03, with supprt at 89.95 then 88.52 and 87.78.

Our next article will be published on Sunday. Until then, we wish you well for the week ahead. If you have any questions about anything covered here, please get in touch. We’re always happy to hear from you.

data.title: How The Greater Fool Theory Fuels Stock Market Bubbles
data.description:
How can a company grow its earnings year after year while its shareholders lose money? In this video, FAST Graphs co-founder Chuck Carnevale draws on Chapter 7 of All Investing Is Value Investing, which he co-authored with Professor Nathan Mauck, to explain how the price you pay can determine how much of a company’s growth shows up in your returns.

The Greater Fool Theory describes what happens when investors pay a price that’s hard to justify based on a company’s earnings because they expect someone else to pay even more. As more buyers take that bet, a stock’s price can climb well above its estimated fair value. When buyers stop paying higher prices, the stock can fall sharply or go sideways for years while earnings catch up.

Chuck uses FAST Graphs to show both outcomes. In the Accenture (ACN) example, earnings grew about 9.5% annually over the period shown, yet an investor who bought at roughly 36 times earnings would have lost about 3.5% annually. Autodesk (ADSK) illustrates how a high starting valuation can hold back returns even without a sustained price decline. During the period Chuck highlights, earnings grew about 23% annually while the stock returned less than 4% annually.

Chuck also uses Ball Corporation (BALL) to explain the three drivers of total return: earnings growth, dividends, and changes in the price-to-earnings multiple. A falling multiple can offset years of earnings growth. Buying at a more reasonable valuation can give investors a better chance of benefiting from that growth.

Watch the video to see how Chuck compares stock prices with earnings and estimated fair value on FAST Graphs. Whether you invest for growth or income, a margin of safety gives you room for error when the business or the market falls short of your expectations.

data.title: Mysteries Of The AI Bubble: Where’s The Consumption?
data.description:
Many of us who have been warning of an AI bubble have raised the prospect of a big hit to consumption if the bubble bursts. We base this concern on the conventional view that there is a stock wealth effect on consumption of roughly 3 cents on a dollar. 

This means that if the market were to lose 30 percent of its value (it lost 50 percent in the collapse of the tech bubble), it would eliminate roughly $24 trillion in stock wealth. With a wealth effect of 3 percent, this would translate into a hit to annual consumption of $720 billion, a bit more than 2 percent of GDP. A hit of this magnitude, coupled with the collapse of the AI investment boom, would almost certainly be large enough to throw the economy into a recession.  

Jason Furman has challenged this view, arguing that it seems that the wealth effect on consumption has been much smaller in the years since the pandemic, just 1 cent on the dollar. He points to the fact that the consumption share of GDP does not seem to be especially high at present, meaning that it doesn’t look like the huge increase in stock wealth in the last five years has had much impact on consumption.

This leaves us with a story where we either believe something has changed in the longstanding relationship between stock wealth and consumption or alternatively, that we are missing something. I’m going to explore the “we are missing something” route.

Specifically, I am not sure that people always see savings and consumption the way economists measure them. In this case, the issue would be how they treat the money they spend on buying a home and related expenses like property tax and insurance. In the GDP accounts, the purchase of a home is treated as investment, a form of savings. Similarly, the monthly mortgage payment, as well as property taxes and insurance, are not counted directly at all. They are supposed to be picked up through owners’ equivalent rent, since these expenses should be among the costs driving up rent.

The definitional issues don’t really matter in terms of accounting for consumption and saving, as long as housing costs track rents more or less closely, as has generally been the case. However, this has not been true since the pandemic. (It also wasn’t the case in the housing bubble.)

As can be seen, adjusted for overall inflation, the cost of buying a house has outpaced the cost of renting by around 20 percent since the pandemic. This means, other things equal, homeowners would be paying about 20 percent more on their monthly mortgage payments, taxes, and insurance than if house prices had just risen in step with rents.1 

Suppose that people acted as though this additional 20 percent they are paying on their mortgage and other related ownership costs were consumption and not investment. In the third quarter of this year, the imputed value of owners’ equivalent rent (OER) was $2,652 billion. If this were increased by 20 percent, in line with the gap between house prices and rent, that would increase spending on OER by $530 billion, or 1.6 percent of GDP. It would imply a corresponding reduction in savings. This adjustment would get us considerably closer to the 3 percent estimate of the wealth effect on consumption.

The relevant issue for a collapse of an AI-driven stock bubble is how a plunge in stock wealth would affect this picture. My speculation is that if we continue to see the stock prices of the big AI companies plunge, eager buyers for expensive houses would vanish, and some current owners look to sell to make up for their reduced stock portfolios. That should lower house prices, a good story in my book. Also, we may see some house owners look to cut spending in other areas if they don’t see their housing wealth as part of their targeted savings. (If house prices fall, then there would be a negative wealth effect on consumption from this as well.)

This story is clearly speculative, and I’m generally inclined to say that we should accept the accounting categories that God gave us. But when we have a seeming anomaly, like a sudden shrinking of the size of the stock wealth effect, it is worth trying to beat up our categories a bit to see if we might be missing something.

  1. Homeowners’ insurance, which is not included in the CPI, has hugely outpaced the overall inflation rate over the last decade, presumably due in large part to the effects of global warming. The larger amount that people are now spending on homeowners’ insurance would not directly affect consumption and savings. It would only be picked up indirectly through its effect on owners equivalent rent.
